P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46
STATE OF NEW JERSEY
BEFORE THE PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS COMMISSION
In the Matter of
MOUNT LAUREL BOARD OF EDUCATION,
Petitioner,
-and- Docket No. SN-2026-026
MOUNT LAUREL EDUCATION ASSOCIATION,
Respondent.
SYNOPSIS
The Public Employment Relations Commission denies the
Board’s request for a restraint of binding arbitration of the
Association’s grievance challenging the Board’s denial of sick
leave and loss of pay for employees who did not submit doctor’s
notes when they sought to use sick leave for absences on the day
after the Super Bowl and/or on the day of the Super Bowl Parade.
The Commission finds that sick leave verification policies
requiring the submission of a doctor’s note are non-negotiable.
However, the Commission holds that the application of such
policies, including sick leave denial and the imposition of
penalties such as loss of pay, are legally arbitrable.
This synopsis is not part of the Commission decision. It
has been prepared for the convenience of the reader. It has been
neither reviewed nor approved by the Commission.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46
STATE OF NEW JERSEY
BEFORE THE PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS COMMISSION
In the Matter of
MOUNT LAUREL BOARD OF EDUCATION,
Petitioner,
-and- Docket No. SN-2026-026
MOUNT LAUREL EDUCATION ASSOCIATION,
Respondent.
Appearances:
For the Petitioner, Capehart Scatchard, P.A., attorneys
(Sanmathi Dev, of counsel)
For the Respondent, Selikoff & Cohen, P.A., attorneys
(Steven R. Cohen, of counsel; Hop T. Wechsler, of
counsel)
DECISION
On March 31, 2026, the Mount Laurel Board of Education
(Board) filed a scope of negotiations petition seeking a
restraint of binding arbitration of a grievance filed by the
Mount Laurel Education Association (Association). The grievance
challenges the Board’s denial of sick leave and deduction of a
day’s pay for three staff members who did not provide a doctor’s
note when they sought to use sick leave for their absences on
February 10, 2025 and/or February 14, 2025.
The Board filed a brief with exhibits and the certification
of its counsel attesting to the truth and accuracy of the

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 2.
exhibits, as well as a reply brief. The Association filed a
brief and a sur-reply brief.1/ These facts appear.
The Association represents the Board’s certified teachers,
secretaries, custodians, assistants, library aides, nurse aides,
office aides, preschool handicap aides, aides to classrooms,
aides to classrooms, applied behavior analysis trainers, signing
interpreter, technology support specialist, occupational
therapist, intervener for deaf and blind, and other titles listed
in the recognition clause of the parties’ collective negotiations
agreement (CNA). The Board and Association are parties to a CNA
with a term of July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2027.
Article 7 of the CNA sets forth the parties’ grievance
procedure. Article 7.A.1. defines a grievance as “a claim by an
employee or the Association based upon the interpretation,
application, or violation of this agreement, policies or
administrative decisions affecting terms and conditions of
employment.” The grievance procedure ends in binding
arbitration. Article 4 of the CNA is entitled “Employee Rights.”
Article 4.E. is entitled “Just Cause Provision” and provides that
no teacher or educational support personnel shall be disciplined
without just cause and that any discipline “shall be subject to
the grievance procedure.”
1/ N.J.A.C. 19:13-3.6(f) requires that all pertinent facts be
supported by certifications based upon personal knowledge.
Neither party submitted such a certification.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 3.
The Board’s Sick and Personal Leave Policy 4150/4250
provides that it “reserves the right to specify the conditions
under which leaves and absences may be taken when not otherwise
covered by the terms of a negotiated agreement.” The Policy
provides, in pertinent part:
The board reserves the right to require
sufficient proof of any professional staff
member claiming sick leave pay, including a
physician’s certification, of the
professional staff member’s illness or
disability.
Any professional staff member absent on sick
leave may be required to submit a physician’s
written statement certifying his or her
disability. Such statements may not be
presumed to establish the professional staff
member’s disability conclusively.
On February 7, 2025, in anticipation of the Philadelphia
Eagles potentially winning the Super Bowl on February 9, the
Board’s Superintendent issued a memorandum to staff entitled
“Super Bowl and Parade Absenteeism Protocols.” The memorandum
notified staff that it was “implementing protocols for the use of
sick leave for the day after the Super Bowl (Monday, February 10,
2025), as well as for the potential celebratory parade day (TBD),
should the Eagles claim victory.” The memorandum provided:
In order to address absenteeism on these
dates, we will require a doctor’s note for
anyone who calls out sick for their own
personal illness or injury. If a doctor’s
note is not provided for the aforementioned
dates your sick leave will not be approved
and subsequently will result in a dockage of
pay. Personal leave requests are being

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 4.
addressed according to district policy and
collective bargaining agreements.
On May 30, 2025, the Board’s Director of Human Resources
sent separate letters to three Association unit employees
reiterating the February 7 memorandum concerning absences the day
after the Super Bowl, and stating:
Our records show that you were absent on
Monday, February 10, 2025 to which you used a
sick day and did not provide a medical note.
I reached out to you on February 11, 2025 and
again on February 18, 2025 to request this
medical note to which you have been unable to
provide. Subsequently, your June 15, 2025
payroll will result in a day without pay of
your per diem amount of [applicable $
amount]. If this was an oversight on your
part and you indeed can provide a medical
note for your absence, please promptly
forward that medical note to my attention
before Monday, June 2, 2025 to avoid this
payroll dockage.
On June 16, 2025, the Association filed a grievance
contesting the payroll deductions for the three unit employees
for their sick day following the Eagles’ Super Bowl victory.2/
The grievance asserts that the CNA provides that while employees
may be asked to provide a sick note, it is silent on any pay
deduction due to no documentation for that sick day. The
2/ While the Board’s May 30, 2025 letters indicate February 10
(the day after the Super Bowl) as the absences for these
employees, the Association’s grievance references February
14 absences (the day of the Super Bowl Parade), and the
Board’s response to the grievance clarifies that for one
staff member the absence without a doctor’s note was
February 10 and for the other two it was February 14.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 5.
Association further argues there is no past practice of
withholding pay for an employee sick day without documentation.
On June 27, the Superintendent denied the grievance, noting that
when an employee’s absence has not been approved, “the District
has designated such a day as an unpaid day.” On July 2, the
Association advanced the grievance to the Board, asserting that
“[t]here is not a district policy or an agreement with the MLEA
that allows the district to dock a member’s pay because they
cannot provide a doctor’s note for a one day absence, due to
illness.” On July 9, the Board, through its counsel, denied the
grievance. On August 7, the Association filed a request for
binding arbitration. This petition ensued.
The Commission’s inquiry on a scope of negotiations
petition is quite narrow. We are addressing a single issue in
the abstract: whether the subject matter in dispute is within the
scope of collective negotiations. The merits of the
Association’s claimed violation of the agreement, as well as the
Board’s contractual defenses, are not in issue, because those are
matters for the arbitrator to decide if the Commission determines
that the question is one that may be arbitrated. Ridgefield Park
Ed. Ass’n v. Ridgefield Park Bd. of Ed., 78 N.J. 144, 154 (1978).
Local 195, IFPTE v. State, 88 N.J. 393 (1982), articulates
the standards for determining whether a subject is mandatorily
negotiable:

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 6.
[A] subject is negotiable between public
employers and employees when (1) the item
intimately and directly affects the work and
welfare of public employees; (2) the subject
has not been fully or partially preempted by
statute or regulation; and (3) a negotiated
agreement would not significantly interfere
with the determination of governmental
policy. To decide whether a negotiated
agreement would significantly interfere with
the determination of governmental policy, it
is necessary to balance the interests of the
public employees and the public employer.
When the dominant concern is the government’s
managerial prerogative to determine policy, a
subject may not be included in collective
negotiations even though it may intimately
affect employees’ working conditions.
[Id. at 404-405].
We must balance the parties’ interests in light of the particular
facts and arguments presented. City of Jersey City v. Jersey
City POBA, 154 N.J. 555, 574-575 (1998).
The Board asserts it has a managerial prerogative to verify
sick leave with a physician’s note and that N.J.S.A. 18A:30-4
also provides it with the right to maintain and enforce a sick
leave verification requirement. The Board argues that it has a
non-negotiable and non-arbitrable managerial prerogative to deny
paid sick leave when an employee fails to comply with the sick
leave verification procedure by not providing a doctor’s note.
The Board contends that the Association’s grievance “seeks to
avoid the natural consequences of violating the sick leave
policy.” The Board asserts that allowing negotiation over its

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 7.
sick leave verification policy would significantly interfere with
its governmental policy interest in reducing staff absenteeism.
The Association asserts that while the employer’s
establishment of a sick leave verification policy is a managerial
prerogative, the employer’s application of that policy -
including whether an employee was properly denied sick leave - is
legally arbitrable. It argues that the Board incorrectly
characterizes the grievance as a challenge to the Board’s sick
leave verification policy rather than a challenge to the Board’s
denial of sick leave and docking of a day’s pay for three
employees who were sick but did not see a doctor. The
Association contends that this case is nearly identical to a
previous Commission case involving the denial of sick leave to an
employee who did not provide a doctor’s note for the day of the
Super Bowl Parade in 2018 following the Eagles’ previous Super
Bowl victory. It asserts that the Commission must similarly find
here that the Association can arbitrate the application of the
sick leave verification policy, i.e., the denial of sick leave.
N.J.S.A. 18A:30-4 establishes a board’s ability to require a
physician’s certificate to verify sick leave. Moreover, it is
well-settled that a public employer has a managerial prerogative
to use reasonable means to verify employee illness, including
requiring the production of a doctor’s note. See e.g., Carteret
Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 2009-71, 35 NJPER 213 (¶76 2009); N.J.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 8.
State Judiciary (Ocean Vicinage), P.E.R.C. No. 2005-24, 30 NJPER
436 (¶143 2004); North Hudson Reg. Fire and Rescue, P.E.R.C. No.
2000-78, 26 NJPER 184 (¶31075 2000); City of Elizabeth, P.E.R.C.
No. 2000-42, 26 NJPER 22 (¶31007 1999); and Piscataway Tp. Bd. of
Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 82-64, 8 NJPER 95 (¶13039 1982).
However, the application of a sick leave verification
policy, e.g., whether an employee was improperly denied sick
leave, the imposition of economic sanctions such as denial of
pay, and whether just cause existed for the imposition of
disciplinary penalties for violating sick leave or absenteeism
policies, may be challenged through contractual grievance
procedures including binding arbitration. City of Burlington Bd.
of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 2019-27, 45 NJPER 242 (¶64 2019), aff’d,
2019 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 2422, 46 NJPER 226 (¶52 App. Div.
2019), certif. den., 241 N.J. 82 (2020); Monroe Tp. Bd. of Ed.,
P.E.R.C. No. 2020-51, 46 NJPER 518 (¶115 2020) (grievance
alleging “arbitrary docking of some employees’ pay” for
attendance policy violation is arbitrable); N. Hudson Reg.,
P.E.R.C. No. 2000-78, supra (“the penalties for violating sick
leave and absenteeism policies, are mandatorily negotiable”);
Elizabeth, P.E.R.C. No. 2000-42, supra (“arbitration may be
invoked” for disciplinary sanctions for absenteeism including
“docking of pay”); State of New Jersey (Treasury), P.E.R.C. No.
95-67, 21 NJPER 129 (¶26080 1995) (“what the disciplinary

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 9.
penalties will be for abusing sick leave” is mandatorily
negotiable); and Piscataway, P.E.R.C. No. 82-64, supra (“The
application of the [sick leave verification] policy, however, may
be subject to contractual grievance procedures.”)
In Teaneck Tp., P.E.R.C. No. 93-44, 19 NJPER 18 (¶24009
1992), the Commission confirmed that an employer does not need to
negotiate over “a policy of denying sick leave benefits to
employees who fail to comply with a verification requirement.”
19 NJPER at 19-20, n. 3. However, the Commission clarified that
the imposition of that policy could still be contested in
arbitration, not just based on claims of compliance with the sick
leave verification policy, but also based on claims for why there
could not be compliance. The Commission stated:
In addition, a union may arbitrate claims
that particular denials of benefits violated
the contract because an employee justifiably
could not comply with the verification
requirement or because the employee complied
and benefits were nevertheless denied. We
therefore decline to restrain arbitration to
the extent, if any, the grievance raises
these issues.
[Teaneck, 19 NJPER at 19.]
In Burlington City Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 2019-27, supra,
the school board e-mailed staff notifying them that if they do
not come to work on February 8, 2018 (the day of the Eagles’
Super Bowl Parade) due to personal illness, then they “will be
required to provide a doctor’s note that indicates that you were

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 10.
unable to come to work due to illness.” An employee was absent
on the day of the Super Bowl Parade due to personal illness.
After the board requested a doctor’s note to verify his illness,
he responded that he did not see a doctor because he had the flu
and they do not want people with the flu in their offices. The
board denied his sick leave for February 8 and advised him it
would be either an unpaid leave absence or a personal business
absence. The union filed a grievance challenging the denial of
sick leave for that employee and all similarly situated
employees. The board filed a petition seeking to restrain
binding arbitration. The Commission, although finding that the
board has a statutory and managerial right to require a doctor’s
note to verify sick leave, denied the board’s request to restrain
arbitration. Citing Commission precedent holding that “the
application of a sick leave verification policy . . . may be
challenged through contractual grievance procedures,” we found
that the grievance challenged the denial of the employee’s sick
leave after he failed to obtain a doctor’s note, not the board’s
right to establish the sick leave verification policy.
On appeal, the Appellate Division affirmed the Commission’s
decision and the arbitrability of challenges to the application
of sick leave verification policies. The Court held:
Whether an employer may impose a disciplinary
penalty in applying a sick leave verification
policy may be reviewed through binding
arbitration. New Jersey State Judiciary

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 11.
(Ocean Vicinage), P.E.R.C. No. 2005-24, 30
NJPER ¶143, 2004 N.J. PERC LEXIS 168 at 9-10
(2004). The Board argued PERC erred in
allowing arbitration of its non-negotiable
right to establish a sick leave verification
policy. However, that is not the subject of
the Association’s grievance. The Association
challenged the application of the sick leave
verification policy to Association members
absent on February 8, 2018. . . . PERC’s
decision that the Association’s grievance is
arbitrable is fully supported by the evidence
in the record.
[Burlington City Bd. of Ed., 2019 N.J. Super.
Unpub. LEXIS 2422, *7-8.]
Here, as in Burlington City Bd. of Ed., the Association has
clarified that its grievance does not challenge the Board’s
managerial prerogative to request doctor’s notes to verify sick
leave absences on the day of the Eagles Super Bowl Parade.3/
Rather, similar to Burlington, the Association’s grievance
challenges the application of the Board’s sick leave verification
policy, specifically the deduction of a day’s pay from the
paychecks of three employees who did not provide a doctor’s note
for the days they sought to use sick leave during the week after
the Eagles’ 2025 Super Bowl victory. Accordingly, consistent
with Burlington and the above-cited Commission precedent, the
Association’s grievance is legally arbitrable. See, e.g., Monroe
Tp. Bd. of Ed.; N. Hudson Reg.; Elizabeth; State of New Jersey
(Treasury); Piscataway, and Teaneck.
3/ Or, in this case, additionally for the day after the Super
Bowl for one employee.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 12.
Finally, we find the Board’s reliance on City of Newark,
P.E.R.C. No. 85-26, 10 NJPER 551 (¶15256 1984), to be misplaced.
In that case, certain employees did not sign new forms the board
was requiring employees to complete to certify to the reasons for
their requested sick or funeral leave. The case did not involve
the application of a policy requiring the submission of a
doctor’s note, and sick and funeral leave benefits were not
denied based on the employees’ noncompliance. Rather, the
Commission found that the certification form was a “reasonable
and unintrusive requirement,” that “has only a slight and
unintrusive impact on the teachers’ work and welfare” while
supporting the board’s interest in combating sick leave abuse.
The Commission noted that its result was limited to restraining
arbitration based on sick leave being denied for the sole reason
that employees refused to certify their absences were due to
illness or due to a funeral, stating: “We stress that our result
is predicated on the limited and undisputed facts of this case.”
Newark, 10 NJPER at 552; see also Troy v. Rutgers, 168 N.J. 354,
383 (2001) (“Questions concerning whether subjects are
mandatorily negotiable should be made on a case-by-case basis.”)
As Newark is factually distinguishable from the instant case and
constrained by its particular circumstances, we do not find it to
be persuasive precedent. By contrast, Burlington, decided much

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 13.
more recently and affirmed by the Appellate Division, is nearly
identical factually to the circumstances herein.
ORDER
The request of the Mount Laurel Board of Education for a
restraint of binding arbitration of the Mount Laurel Education
Association’s grievance is denied.
BY ORDER OF THE COMMISSION
Chair Hennessy-Shotter, Commissioners Eaton, Davey, Hines, and
Papero voted in favor of this decision. None opposed.
Commissioner Higgins was not present.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-45
STATE OF NEW JERSEY
BEFORE THE PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS COMMISSION
In the Matter of
SOUTH ORANGE-MAPLEWOOD BOARD
OF EDUCATION,
Petitioner,
-and- Docket No. SN-2026-019
SOUTH ORANGE-MAPLEWOOD EDUCATION
ASSOCIATION,
Respondent.
SYNOPSIS
The Public Employment Relations Commission grants the
Board's request for a restraint of binding arbitration of the
Association's grievance, alleging that the Board violated the
parties' CNA by assigning non-negotiated duties to teachers
outside of scheduled lunch periods. To the extent the
Association contests the assignment of these duties, the
Commission finds that the grievance is not legally arbitrable
because the assignment of these duties is related to student
safety and supervision. The Commission further finds that
Association has not established that the Board’s assigned
supervisory duties have adversely impacted the teachers’
compensation, workload, or preparation time, and thus, this
record does not establish severable impact issues that could be
arbitrable.
This synopsis is not part of the Commission decision. It
has been prepared for the convenience of the reader. It has been
neither reviewed nor approved by the Commission.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-45
STATE OF NEW JERSEY
BEFORE THE PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS COMMISSION
In the Matter of
SOUTH ORANGE-MAPLEWOOD BOARD
OF EDUCATION,
Petitioner,
-and- Docket No. SN-2026-019
SOUTH ORANGE-MAPLEWOOD EDUCATION
ASSOCIATION,
Respondent.
Appearances:
For the Petitioner, Lenox, Socey, Formidoni, Giordano,
Carrigg, Lang & Casey, LLC, attorneys (Patrick F.
Carrigg, of counsel; Victoria R. Lang, on the brief)
For the Respondent, Selikoff & Cohen, P.A., attorneys
(Keith Waldman, of counsel and on the brief; Liz Pudel,
on the brief)
DECISION
On November 19, 2025, the South Orange-Maplewood Board of
Education (Board) filed a scope of negotiations petition seeking
a restraint of binding arbitration of a grievance filed by the
South Orange-Maplewood Education Association (Association). The
grievance asserts that the Board violated Article XXI(7)(g) of
the parties’ collective negotiations agreement (CNA) by assigning
non-negotiated duties (corridor duty, office support duty, and
content lab area duty) to teachers outside of scheduled lunch
periods.
The Board filed briefs, exhibits, and the certification of

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-45 2.
its Superintendent. The Association filed a brief and the
certification of its Chairperson for the Professional Rights and
Responsibilities Committee (Association Chairperson). These
facts appear.
The Association represents certified teaching employees and
non-certified supportive employees. The Board and Association
were parties to a CNA with a term from July 1, 2021 through June
30, 2024, which continues in effect. The grievance procedure
ends in binding arbitration.
Article XXI(7)(g) of the parties’ CNA, entitled “Employee
Hours and Employee Work Load,” provides in pertinent part:
All middle school teachers shall be assigned
to one daily - related duty period, which may
include cafeteria and/or corridor. The duty
assignment shall be rotated among all middle
school teachers so that a teacher will not be
required to perform more than one duty per
school week. Rotation is intended to be no
more than once every five school days
distributed on an equitable basis.
The Superintendent certifies that the Association initiated
a “Level I” oral grievance concerning a teacher’s assignment to
non-instructional duties of corridor duty, office supervision
duty, and content area lab duty. That grievance was denied.
On September 7, 2025, the Association elevated the grievance
to Level II. On September 16, the Level II grievance was denied,
as follows:
Our assigned duties support safe supervision
of students and allow us to carry out Board

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-45 3.
Policy 3280 excerpted below.
1. Each teaching staff member shall
maintain a standard of care for member’s
assigned duties and responsibilities.
2. A teaching staff member shall not
voluntarily assume responsibility for duties
he or she cannot reasonably perform. Such
assumed responsibilities carry the same
potential for liability as do assigned
responsibilities.
All assigned staff duties for the 2025-2026
school year support the safety of students.
[Exhibit D, Board. Cert. Emphasis added.]
The grievance was then elevated to Level III. On October 1,
2025, the Superintendent denied the grievance, citing Commission
precedent and stating in pertinent part:
Consistent with these precedents, the
District’s assignment of corridor duty,
office supervision duty, and content area lab
duty is a substitution of one student-
supervision location for another within the
middle school. These duties are student
supervisory in nature and directly tied to
the District’s responsibility to ensure
student safety, security, and appropriate
conduct.
Therefore, as the grievance seeks to prevent
District administration from exercising its
managerial prerogative to assign duties
necessary for student supervision and safety,
the grievance is respectfully denied.
[Exhibit E, Board Cert. Emphasis added.]
On October 3, 2025, the Association filed a “Level IV”

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-45 4.
grievance,1/ stating in pertinent part:
[The Board] has directed teachers to perform
duties that are not in the [CNA]. These
duties include corridor duty, office support
duty, and content area lab duty and they are
scheduled to occur outside of the scheduled
lunch periods. They do not comply with the
defined lunch-related duties in the contract.
* * *
Remedies Sought:
1. [The Board] cease and desist immediately
the practice of assigning non-negotiated
duties.
2. [The Board] provide compensation at the
class coverage rate for the members who have
performed these duties....
[Exhibit F, Board Cert.]
On October 30, 2025, the Board held a public board meeting
in which it, by resolution, denied the Level IV grievance in part
and affirmed it in part, stating in pertinent part:
WHEREAS, it has been determined that the
assigned duties constitute reasonable and
necessary supervisory responsibilities
inherent to the role of teaching staff
members and do not violate the specific
provisions cited, as they are not deemed
“lunch-related duties” that infringe upon the
contractually defined duty-free lunch period;
* * *
Maplewood Middle School will cease the
assignment of the office support duty. The
other duty assignments are student
1/ This is the first written statement in the instant record
articulating the Association’s grievance.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-45 5.
supervisory duties that are not subject to
negotiations and may be assigned by the
administration.
The Association Chairperson’s 8-paragraph certification
contains one paragraph addressing the grievance at issue.2/ That
paragraph states only that the Association’s grievance is
“challenging the unilateral imposition of non-instructional
duties on teaching staff members, including but not limited to
office supervision duty.”3/
On November 12, 2025, the Association filed a Request for
Submission of a Panel of Arbitrators, which identifies the
grievance to be arbitrated as, “Principal directed teachers to
perform duties outside the time defined in the collective
bargaining agreement.” This petition ensued.
Our jurisdiction is narrow. The Commission is addressing
the abstract issue of whether the subject matter in dispute is
within the scope of collective negotiations. We do not consider
the merits of the grievance or any contractual defenses that the
employer may have. Ridgefield Park Ed. Ass’n v. Ridgefield Park
Bd. of Ed., 78 N.J. 144, 154 (1978).
2/ The remainder of the certification pertains to other
Association grievances.
3/ As noted above, the Board’s October 30 resolution
discontinued the assignment of “office support duty,”
thereby granting that aspect of the Association’s grievance,
but stated that the remaining assignments are student
supervisory duties.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-45 6.
The Supreme Court of New Jersey articulated the standards
for determining whether a subject is mandatorily negotiable in
Local 195, IFPTE v. State, 88 N.J. 393, 404-405 (1982):
[A] subject is negotiable between public
employers and employees when (1) the item
intimately and directly affects the work and
welfare of public employees; (2) the subject
has not been fully or partially preempted by
statute or regulation; and (3) a negotiated
agreement would not significantly interfere
with the determination of governmental
policy. To decide whether a negotiated
agreement would significantly interfere with
the determination of governmental policy, it
is necessary to balance the interests of the
public employees and the public employer.
When the dominant concern is the government’s
managerial prerogative to determine policy, a
subject may not be included in collective
negotiations even though it may intimately
affect employees’ working conditions.
We must balance the parties’ interests in light of the
particular facts and arguments presented. City of Jersey City v.
Jersey City POBA, 154 N.J. 555, 574-575 (1998).
The Board argues that the Association’s grievance is not
arbitrable because it significantly interferes with its
managerial prerogative to assign teaching staff duties related to
student safety and supervision. The Board asserts these duties -
corridor and content-area lab duty - are not clerical, custodial,
or tangential, but are connected to the Board’s obligation to
protect students and safely operate the school. The Board argues
that “corridor duty” ensures safe student movement between
classes and “lab duty” requires oversight of students in

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-45 7.
environments involving specialized equipment with heightened
safety considerations. The Board further argues that the
assigned safety duties do not substitute a preparation period for
supervisory duty, but rather, are simply substituting one form of
student supervision (e.g., lunch duty) for another within the
school day.
The Association argues that the grievance is arbitrable
because it is challenging the manner in which these non-
instructional duties are distributed amongst the teachers and the
resulting impacts on the teachers’ compensation, workload, and
preparatory time. The Association asserts these issues are
severable from the non-negotiable assignment of the student
supervision for safety purposes. The Association contends that
the severable and negotiable impacts of the supervision duties
are issues of fact for an arbitrator to determine. The
Association asserts that the method of distributing safety
supervision assignments and compensation for performing them are
mandatorily negotiable and arbitrable, particularly if such
assignments increase workload or reduce preparatory time.
The assignment of non-teaching duties related to student
safety, control, or supervision are not mandatorily negotiable.
Byram Tp. Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 76-27 (1976), aff’d 152 N.J.
Super. 12 (App. Div. 1977). Moreover, employers are not required
to negotiate over “minor tasks incidental to [a public

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-45 8.
employee’s] primary duties.” Bayonne Bd. of Ed. P.E.R.C. No. 87-
109, 13 NJPER 268 (¶18110 1987); see also New Jersey Highway
Auth. v. IFPTE Local 193 (Toll Supervisors of Am.), AFL-CIO, 2003
N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 20 (App. Div. 2003). However, the
method of distributing these assignments, compensation for
performing them, as well as reductions in preparation time and
increases in workload are mandatorily negotiable and arbitrable
issues. Long Branch Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 93-8, 18 NJPER 403
(¶23182 1992).
The documented responses of the Board throughout the
grievance process consistently reflect that the assignment of
non-teaching duties in the instant dispute is related to safety
and student supervision. Thus, based on the above cited
precedent, to the extent the Association contests the assignment
of these duties, the grievance is not legally arbitrable.
The Association’s Level IV grievance also seeks compensation
for performing these non-teaching duties. However, the Board’s
response to the Level III grievance, and the Superintendent’s
certification, provide that these supervisory duties do not
increase the teacher’s student supervision time and are “a
substitution of one student-supervision location [e.g. lunch
duty] for another within the middle school.” In contrast, the
Association’s certification contains no support that the
teachers’ workload or compensation has been impacted by these

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-45 9.
supervisory assignments.4/ Compare Ocean Cty. Vocational
Technical Sch. P.E.R.C. No. 2019-29, 45 NJPER 301 (¶78
2019)(denying a restraint of arbitration of a grievance
challenging a secretary’s assignment of breakfast duties without
additional compensation, where she certified that her
compensation and workload were impacted.); see also Tp. of
Lyndhurst, P.E.R.C. No. 2017-41, 43 NJPER 301 (¶85
2017)(restraining arbitration of a grievance challenging a
Township ordinance restricting off-duty police work because the
Association did not produce any evidence of claimed severable
impact issues.); Clark Tp., P.E.R.C. No. 2016-55, 42 NJPER 372
(¶105 2016), aff’d, No. A-2544-15T3, 2016 N.J. Super. Unpub.
LEXIS 2348 (App. Div. Oct. 28, 2016)(restraining arbitration
regarding alleged severable impact issues because the union did
not produce any evidence demonstrating that the grievant’s
workload increased as a result of the Township’s unilateral
change to her work hours/schedule.)
We acknowledge Commission precedent cited by the Association
supporting that a grievance may develop as it proceeds through
the grievance process.5/ However, that precedent is not
4/ We also note that the Association provided no support for a
severable compensation claim for the office duty that was
discontinued by the Board.
5/ The Commission determines scope of negotiations petitions
based on the totality of the certified facts and arguments
(continued...)

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-45 10.
applicable to the instant matter where the Association has not
certified to severable impacts from the disputed assignments. In
the absence of certified facts from the Association that the
Board’s assigned supervisory duties have adversely impacted the
teachers’ compensation, workload, or preparation time, this
record is insufficient to establish severable impact issues.
For the foregoing reasons, we grant the Board’s request for
a restraint of binding arbitration of the Association’s
grievance.
ORDER
South Orange-Maplewood Board of Education’s request for a
restraint of binding arbitration is granted.
BY ORDER OF THE COMMISSION
Chair Hennessy-Shotter, Commissioners Eaton, Davey, Hines, and
Papero voted in favor of this decision. None opposed.
Commissioner Higgins was not present.
ISSUED: June 25, 2026
Trenton, New Jersey
5/ (...continued)
raised by the parties and has often acknowledged that a
dispute becomes more sharply focused as the grievance
proceeds and professional assistance is received at higher
levels of the grievance process. See North Hunterdon Reg.
H.S. Dist. Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 86-55, 11 NJPER 707, n.3
(¶16245 1985).

STATE OF NEW JERSEY

In the Matter of
COUNTY OF GLOUCESTER,
Petitioner,
-and- Docket No. SN-2026-020
CWA LOCAL 1085,
Respondent.
SYNOPSIS
The Public Employment Relations Commission grants the
request of the County of Gloucester for a restraint of binding
arbitration of grievances filed by CWA Local 1085 contesting the
County’s decisions not to hire the grievant, a part-time Public
Safety Telecommunicator (PST), to certain full-time positions.
The Commission finds this dispute concerns the grievant not being
transferred or reassigned to a full-time PST position or selected
for the full-time fire-room position that he applied for. The
Commission finds those claims are not legally arbitrable because
employers have a managerial prerogative to make hiring decisions
to meet the governmental policy goal of matching the best
qualified employees to particular jobs. The Commission further
finds the record does not support CWA’s argument that the dispute
concerns the negotiability of the grievant’s individual work
schedule. The Commission denies the County’s petition only to
the extent the grievances seek an explanation as to why the
grievant was not selected for the desired positions.
This synopsis is not part of the Commission decision. It
has been prepared for the convenience of the reader. It has been
neither reviewed nor approved by the Commission.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-43
STATE OF NEW JERSEY
BEFORE THE PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS COMMISSION
In the Matter of
COUNTY OF GLOUCESTER,
Petitioner,
-and- Docket No. SN-2026-020
CWA LOCAL 1085,
Respondent.
Appearances:
For the Petitioner, Brown & Connery, LLP, attorneys
(Michael J. DiPiero, of counsel)
For the Respondent, Weissman & Mintz, LLC, attorneys
(Ira W. Mintz, of counsel)
DECISION
On November 21, 2025, the County of Gloucester (County)
filed a scope of negotiations petition seeking a restraint of
binding arbitration of two grievances filed by CWA Local 1085
(CWA). The grievances assert that the County violated the
parties’ collective negotiations agreement (CNA) by failing to
hire the grievant as a full-time Public Safety Telecommunicator
(PST) or a full-time Police Dispatcher. The County filed briefs,
exhibits, and the certification of its counsel, Michael J.
DiPiero. CWA filed a brief.1/ These facts appear.2/
1/ N.J.A.C. 19:13-3.6(f) requires that all pertinent facts be
supported by certifications based upon personal knowledge.
CWA did not file a certification, and the County’s
certification from its counsel only recites procedural facts
(continued...)

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-43 2.
The County and CWA are parties to a CNA in effect from
January 1, 2024, through December 31, 2028. The grievance
procedure ends in binding arbitration. CWA represents all full-
time employees in the Blue and White Collar, Supervisory, and Row
Office negotiations units, including craft employees, Mosquito
Control employees, Emergency Medical Technicians, and
investigators in the Medical Examiner’s Office.3/ Part-time
employees in the above categories are also included.
The CNA states that the employer “reserves sole
determination to make promotional appointments,” and that
employees seeking promotion “must possess the skill, knowledge,
and potential ability to learn the job within a reasonable time,
to be determined by the Employer.” (CNA, Art. 26.2.) The CNA
also states that seniority will be considered before an
appointment is made, “[w]hen qualifications are substantially
equal.” (Id.)
The grievant is employed in the County’s Emergency Response
Department as a part-time PST. In a series of emails in late
1/ (...continued)
and identifies attached exhibits.
2/ Although the CNA’s recognition clause refers to “bargaining
units,” we will use the term “negotiations units,”
consistent with the terminology of our Act as it applies to
public employment relations. See, e.g., N.J.S.A. 34:13A-
5.12.
3/ The grievant’s title of “Public Safety Telecommunicator” is
not listed in the recognition clause. However, the CNA
elsewhere refers to employees in the “PST series.” There
appears to be no dispute that the grievant is a unit member.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-43 3.
2024 between the grievant and the County’s Director of Emergency
Response (Director), the grievant notified the County that he was
retiring from his full-time position with another public employer
and inquired about the possibility of getting a full-time
position with the County. If possible, the grievant requested
that the full-time position be in a leadership role within the
County’s Office of Emergency Management (OEM).
In the course of this email exchange, the Director informed
the grievant there was no full-time position currently available.
He also advised that the County’s Deputy Director/OEM Coordinator
had “been asking to bring on additional OEM staff and is
strenuously arguing for some young, eager to learn and willing to
work bodies (as opposed to retired police or Fire guys/girls”).
Moreover, he informed the grievant that he nevertheless
“present[ed himself] extremely well and certainly h[as] the
requisite experience” for a leadership/management position. On
December 18, 2024, the County’s Training Coordinator notified the
grievant that the Director was taking measures to have him placed
on the full-time list.
On January 16, 2025, the Director notified the grievant that
despite his endorsement, he was told at a Director’s meeting that
the grievant would not be moved into a full-time position. The
next day he advised the grievant that there was no discussion or
explanation about that decision. On January 27, the Director
again notified the grievant that he had no further explanation

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-43 4.
for the decision.
On February 19, 2025, CWA filed a grievance alleging:
Grievant is a 22 year part-time PST and has
been seeking a full-time position. Grievant
has had multiple meetings with the
department’s management, and despite his
request to move to full time, the department
has posted a CWA job announcement dated
2/11/25 for more full-time PST trainees.
Grievant is an experienced PST with a good
work record and no past discipline and should
receive any full-time opening over an
inexperienced trainee.
As a remedy, CWA sought that the grievant be given the first
available full-time Public Safety Telecommunicator position that
is open in Emergency Response.
On May 16, 2025, CWA filed a second grievance on behalf of
the grievant alleging:
GC PSTs received an email notifying them of a
full-time opening in the EMS/Fire room,
stating the opening was for “any police room
dispatchers interested in voluntarily
switching to the fire room on a full-time
basis.” Notification also states the
department would abide by the contract and
everything would be done by seniority.
Although grievant is not a police room
dispatcher, he requested the position and
would not require any of the offered
training. Grievant was told his “desire” was
previously sent to Woodbury, disregarding the
grievant’s request for the current opening.
The May 16 grievance requested as a remedy that the grievant “be
given the full-time opening advertised to employees unless there
is another more qualified PST with more seniority than the
grievant.”

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-43 5.
According to facts alleged in its brief, the County denied
both grievances, asserting as a basis for the denials that it
“had chosen candidates it felt were more qualified for the full-
time positions.”4/
On July 15, 2025, CWA filed two separate Requests for
Submission of a Panel of Arbitrators (AR-2026-024; AR-2026-025),
respectively seeking arbitration of the February 19 and May 16
grievances. The request form for AR-2026-025 contains the
following statement identifying the February 19 grievance:
Grievant is a 22-year part-time PST and was
passed over for a full-time opening posted on
2/11/25 despite having over twenty [years] of
experience over all employees who were
eventually given the position.
The request form for AR-2026-024 identifies the May 16 grievance
as follows:
Grievant is a 22-year part-time PST and
received a 5/9/25 work email from the
employer advertising for a full-time position
that the grievant was already working in as a
part-time employee. Despite the employer
stating in the email that the contract would
be followed in regard to seniority, grievant
was denied an interview and the position
despite having both seniority and experience
over the employee given the position.
This petition ensued.
The Commission’s inquiry into a scope of negotiations
petition is quite narrow. We are addressing a single issue in
4/ The record contains no documents memorializing the denials,
or any specific information about either the full-time
positions or those who were hired into them.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-43 6.
the abstract: whether the subject matter in dispute is within the
scope of collective negotiations. The merits of the union's
claimed violation of the agreement, as well as the employer’s
contractual defenses, are not in issue, because those are matters
for the arbitrator to decide if the Commission determines that
the question is one that may be arbitrated. Ridgefield Park Ed.
Ass’n v. Ridgefield Park Bd. of Ed., 78 N.J. 144, 154 (1978).
Local 195, IFPTE v. State, 88 N.J. 393 (1982), articulates
the standards for determining whether a subject is mandatorily
negotiable:
[A] subject is negotiable between public
employers and employees when (1) the item
intimately and directly affects the work and
welfare of public employees; (2) the subject
has not been fully or partially preempted by
statute or regulation; and (3) a negotiated
agreement would not significantly interfere
with the determination of governmental
policy. To decide whether a negotiated
agreement would significantly interfere with
the determination of governmental policy, it
is necessary to balance the interests of the
public employees and the public employer.
When the dominant concern is the government’s
managerial prerogative to determine policy, a
subject may not be included in collective
negotiations even though it may intimately
affect employees’ working conditions.
[Id. at 404-405].
We must balance the parties’ interests in light of the particular
facts and arguments presented. City of Jersey City v. Jersey
City POBA, 154 N.J. 555, 574-575 (1998).
The County argues that arbitration should be restrained
because hiring decisions are a managerial prerogative and not

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-43 7.
mandatorily negotiable. It asserts that the right to fill or not
fill a vacancy, promote employees, and set promotional criteria
are all non-negotiable. The County argues that even if a
contract term provides preference to senior employees when all
qualifications are equal, the County still retains the right to
determine which candidates are equally qualified. It states that
it assessed all candidates interested in the full-time positions
and selected the best candidates to meet the needs of the
department.
CWA argues that because “the grievant seeks neither to be
hired or to be promoted,” the County’s reliance on its managerial
prerogatives over hiring and promotional decisions is irrelevant.
CWA emphasizes that all the grievant seeks “is an increase in
work hours to full-time.” It asserts that work schedules and
hours of work directly and intimately affect employees. CWA
notes that the County has not stated any facts in the record to
support the need to deny the grievant his request of increased
hours, so the matter is arbitrable.
In reply, the County reiterates its prior arguments and
states that CWA’s argument is irrelevant as hiring decisions,
including the ability to not fill a vacancy, are within
management’s rights and cannot be forced to negotiations.
It is well-settled that public employers have a non-
negotiable right to make promotions, and/or transfer and reassign
employees to meet the governmental policy goal of matching the

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-43 8.
best qualified employees to particular jobs. Such decisions
intimately affect an employer’s ability to manage its workforce
and achieve operational goals. Local 195, 88 N.J. at 417 (1982);
see also Ridgefield Park Ed. Ass’n v. Ridgefield Park Bd of Ed.,
78 N.J. 144, 156–157 (1978). Even in instances where a CNA gives
preference to employees with seniority when all qualifications
are equal, the public employer has the right to determine which,
if any, of the candidates are equally qualified. Edison Tp. Bd.
of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 2015-74, 41 NJPER 495 (¶153 2015).
Initially, we decline CWA’s argument that this dispute
concerns the negotiability of the grievant’s individual work
schedule and not his desire to be hired into a full-time PST
position or promoted into another full-time position.5/ The
record facts show that the crux of this dispute is that the
grievant was not transferred or reassigned to a full-time PST
5/ Work schedules are generally mandatorily negotiable if
agreement on that topic would not significantly interfere
with a governmental policy determination. See, e.g., Union
Cty. College, P.E.R.C. No. 2018-38, 44 NJPER 379 (¶107
2018); Carteret Bor., P.E.R.C. No. 2020-23, 46 NJPER 228
(¶53 2019), aff’d, In re Borough of Carteret, 2021 N.J.
Super. Unpub. LEXIS 695 (App. Div. 2021); Morris Cty.
Prosecutor’s Office, P.E.R.C. No. 2004-75, 30 NJPER 204 (¶76
2004). As explained within this decision, this dispute
centers around the County’s hiring decisions, not the
negotiability of the grievant’s individual work schedule.
However, even if this dispute did concern the negotiability
of the grievant’s individual work schedule, compelling the
County through grievance arbitration to hire, transfer or
reassign grievant to a full-time position would be a
significant interference with a governmental policy
determination when the County has already determined that
other candidates were better qualified.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-43 9.
position or selected for the full-time fire room position that he
applied for. Those claims are not legally arbitrable. As set
forth above, employers have a managerial prerogative to make
hiring decisions to meet the governmental policy goal of matching
the best qualified employees to particular jobs. See, Local 195,
supra; Ridgefield Park, supra. The County states that it
assessed all candidates interested in the full-time positions and
selected the best candidates to meet the needs of the department.
CWA argues that even if this case is about the County’s
right to match the best qualified employees to particular jobs,
the County has failed to provide an explanation of the relative
qualifications of the selected candidates. Indeed, the County
has not provided an explanation as to why the grievant was not
selected for the full-time positions. We have held legally
arbitrable procedures relating to the promotion process including
“the right to know why an employee’s application was rejected,”
as long as such requests do not infringe upon the employer’s
right to exercise its managerial functions. Ocean Cty. Utilities
Auth., P.E.R.C. No. 2011-30, 36 NJPER 367, 369 (¶143 2010). See,
also, Tp. of Nutley, P.E.R.C. No. 88-90, 14 NJPER 254, 255
(¶19095 1988) (employee requests for justification of management
personnel actions are negotiable).6/ To the extent the CWA seeks
6/ Note, however, that since the Legislature’s adoption of the
Civil Service Act in 1986, a Civil Service appointing
authority such as the County cannot be compelled to advise
eligible applicants of reasons they were not selected for
(continued...)

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-43 10.
an explanation as to why the grievant was not selected for the
full-time positions, that issue is legally arbitrable.
Accordingly, the County’s request for a restraint of binding
arbitration is granted, except to the extent CWA seeks an
explanation from the County as to why grievant was not selected
for the full-time positions.
ORDER
The request of the County of Gloucester for a restraint of
binding arbitration is granted, except to the extent the
grievance seeks an explanation as to why the grievant was not
selected for the full-time positions.
BY ORDER OF THE COMMISSION
Chair Hennessy-Shotter, Commissioners Higgins, Hines, and Papero
voted in favor of this decision. Commissioner Davey recused
herself. Commissioner Eaton was not present.
ISSUED: May 28, 2026
Trenton, New Jersey
6/ (...continued)
“rule of three” promotions, i.e., those involving open
competitive examinations wherein the appointing authority
may select one of the three highest scoring candidates.
Local 518, New Jersey State Motor Vehicle Employees Union,
S.E.I.U., AFL-CIO v. Division of Motor Vehicles, 262 N.J.
Super. 598 (App. Div. 1993). The record does not indicate
that the grievances in this case concern “rule of three”
appointments.

appeal of the Director of Unfair Practices’ refusal to issue a
complaint on his unfair practice charge (UPC) against the PBA.

On January 23, 2026, the Charging Party (Leary) filed an
unfair practice charge (UPC) against his union, PBA Mainland
Local 77 (PBA). The UPC alleges that the PBA violated subsection
5.4b(1)1/ of the New Jersey Employer-Employee Relations Act
(Act), N.J.S.A. 34:13A-1, et seq, by suspending Leary from the
PBA in retaliation for his previous filing of a UPC against the
PBA and Egg Harbor Township (Township).2/ Leary’s previous UPC

collective negotiations agreement (CNA) with the Township
regarding access to promotional testing materials and by

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-42 3.
opposition to Leary’s appeal of the dismissal.
Summary of Facts
We summarize the pertinent facts as follows. Leary is a
police officer employed by the Township and has been a dues-
paying member of his majority representative, PBA Local 77, and
the State PBA since the start of his employment in 2003. On July
28, 2023, after the Township denied his grievance related to the
promotional testing process and the PBA refused to advance it to
grievance arbitration, Leary filed his previous UPC against both
the PBA and the Township. On July 30, 2023, Leary also filed a
federal lawsuit against the Township and PBA Local 77 and its
President and Business Agent based on the same factual
allegations as in the previous UPC.
On March 25, 2025, the Director issued D.U.P. No. 2025-10
dismissing Leary’s previous UPC. Leary did not appeal that
dismissal to the Commission. On April 17, Leary withdrew his
federal lawsuit as against PBA Local 77 and its officers. On
July 17, PBA Local 77 and its officers filed a motion for
attorney’s fees with the federal district court. On September 4,
the district court denied the motion for attorneys fees. The
court also dismissed Leary’s federal claim against the Township
and dismissed his state law claims against the Township for lack
of jurisdiction. On September 29, Leary re-filed his state law
claims against the Township in New Jersey Superior Court, where

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-42 4.
it is still pending.
On July 24, 2025, the PBA issued a formal notice of
disciplinary review to Leary. The notice stated, in pertinent
part (emphasis supplied in original):
It has come to our attention that on July 28,
2023, you filed a ULP claim with PERC against
Mainland PBA, Local #77 and PBA President
Jeff Lancaster. Also, on July 30, 2023, you
filed suit in Federal Court against Mainland
PBA, Local 77 and PBA President Jeff
Lancaster for the same accusations. This
behavior resulted in harm, not only to a
fellow union member but your own union as a
whole. Following a preliminary review, this
action is considered a violation of the
Union’s Bylaws, specifically Article XXIX,
Section E: “Oath for New Members.”
The letter stated that the matter was being referred to the PBA’s
Judiciary Review Board for further investigation and that
disciplinary outcomes may include “suspension of union privileges
or expulsion.” In an August 4, 2025 e-mail, the PBA’s State
Delegate notified Leary of the August 20 Judiciary hearing and
reiterated the alleged misconduct as follows:
As stated in the letter you are being charged
with a violation of Article XXIX. section E:
“Oath of New Members” by filing a law suit
against the Local Association and its
president with PERC and with Federal Court.
On November 20, 2025, the PBA President notified Leary that
“the disciplinary hearing has concluded that your conduct
warrants a suspension from the [PBA] for a period of six (6)
months.” The letter set forth multiple membership benefits that

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-42 5.
would be lost, including death benefit coverage, legal protection
plan, eligibility to attend union meetings, voting rights on
union matters, and possession or use of any materials identifying
you as a PBA member. It also stated that at the conclusion of
his six-month suspension, Leary “may petition the membership body
for reinstatement.”
On November 21, 2025, Leary sent a letter to the State PBA
appealing his suspension and requesting a stay. On December 8,
the State PBA Judiciary Committee granted Leary’s request for a
stay of his suspension during the pendency of his appeal. On
January 5, 2026, the State PBA Judiciary Committee decided to
hold the appeal in abeyance pending resolution of Leary’s state
lawsuit against the Township.
Arguments
Leary’s appeal asserts that the Commission should remand his
UPC to the Director for issuance of a Complaint because the PBA’s
suspension of his union membership in retaliation for filing his
previous UPC interfered with his rights under the Act in
violation of N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4b(1). Leary argues that res
judicata and collateral estoppel are inapplicable because he does
not seek to relitigate the same cause of action or factual
allegations that were involved in his previously dismissed UPC.
Leary asserts that the claim in this case is based on the PBA’s
retaliatory suspension that occurred after his previous UPC was

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-42 6.
dismissed and after he had voluntarily withdrawn his related
federal lawsuit against the PBA. Leary asserts the Director also
erred in finding that his appeal to the State PBA and unrelated
state lawsuit against the Township preclude the Commission from
considering his UPC. Leary argues his UPC is not moot because
his suspension has not been rescinded, the pending suspension has
already interfered with his protected rights, and the State PBA’s
eventual decision would not resolve his UPC.
The PBA admits there is no res judicata issue barring
Leary’s UPC because it is not a relitigation of his previous UPC,
but asserts that there would be collateral estoppel of any
allegations “that predate the July 24, 2025 letter commencing the
disciplinary review.” The PBA argues that Leary’s UPC is moot or
unripe while his appeal of his disciplinary suspension is pending
before the State PBA because his suspension is currently being
stayed pending the resolution of that process. The PBA argues
that the UPC could be deferred until the State PBA makes its
decision on Leary’s appeal, but acknowledges that it is holding
that decision in abeyance until resolution of Leary’s state claim
against the Township.
Standard of Review
The Commission has authority to issue a complaint where it
appears that a charging party’s allegations, if true, may
constitute an unfair practice within the meaning of the Act.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-42 7.
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4c; N.J.A.C. 19:14-2.1. Where no complaint is
issued, the charging party may appeal to the Commission, which
may sustain the refusal to issue a complaint or may direct that
further action be taken. N.J.A.C. 19:14-2.3(b).
Analysis
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4b(1) prohibits a union from “interfering
with, restraining, or coercing employees in the exercise of the
rights guaranteed to them by the Act.” A union violates this
proscription when its action tends to interfere with protected
rights and lacks a legitimate and substantial organizational
justification. FOP, Lodge No. 12 (Colisanti), P.E.R.C. No.
90-65, 16 NJPER 126 (¶21049 1990).
Unions may create rules binding on their members to
accomplish organizational objectives, often in the form of
constitutions and by-laws. Calabrese v. PBA Local 76, 157 N.J.
Super. 139 (Law Div. 1978); Danese v. Ginesi, 280 N.J. Super. 17,
25 (App. Div. 1995). “The Commission will not intercede in
intra-union disputes unless they are connected to allegations
that an unfair practice has been committed.” PBA Local 334
(Mendoza), P.E.R.C. No. 2025-3, 51 NJPER 105 (¶25 2024), citing
NJ State PBA & PBA Local 199 (Rinaldo), P.E.R.C. No. 2011-83, 38
NJPER 56 (¶8 2011); City of Jersey City, P.E.R.C. No. 83-32, 8
NJPER 563, 565-566 (¶13260 1982).
The Commission may find a N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4b(1) violation

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-42 8.
where a union excludes or suspends a negotiations unit employee
if its actions were arbitrary, capricious, discriminatory, or
invidious. PBA Local 334 (Mendoza), supra, citing In re
Probation Ass’n (Tortoreto), 442 N.J. Super. 185, 194-196 (App.
Div. 2015) (employee who alleged union financial mismanagement
could challenge union suspension as arbitrary). The Commission
has found such arbitrary, capricious, discriminatory, or
invidious actions could include a union suspending a member after
that member files an unfair practice charge against it. PBA
Local 152 (Smith), P.E.R.C. No. 99-18, 24 NJPER 450 (¶29208 1998)
(union’s reference to UPC as a reason for internal union charges
seeking to suspend employee’s union membership violated the Act
because it “tended to interfere with his protected rights and
lacked a legitimate and substantial organizational
justification”); Eastampton Tp. Ed. Ass’n (MacCarthy), P.E.R.C.
No. 2025-21, 51 NJPER 186 (¶47 2024) (union violated the Act when
it precluded an employee from running for union office because he
had filed a UPC); and PBA Local 334 (Mendoza), supra (where union
cited employee’s UPC as a basis for union charges and suspension,
the Commission denied union’s motion for summary judgment on the
employee’s 5.4b(1) claim).
Here, the PBA’s disciplinary notice to Leary specifically
referenced his “ULP claim with PERC” as a basis for his alleged
violation of the PBA’s bylaws that resulted in the issuance of a

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-42 9.
six-month suspension of his PBA membership and benefits. Leary’s
allegation that the PBA suspended him because he filed a UPC
against it may, if true, violate 5.4b(1) because it has a
tendency to interfere with his protected rights under the Act.
N.J.A.C. 19:14-2.1(a). See PBA Local 152 (Smith), supra;
Eastampton (MacCarthy), supra; PBA Local 334 (Mendoza), supra;
and Probation Ass’n (Tortoreto), supra. Based on the foregoing,
we remand to the Director for the issuance of a complaint on
Leary’s 5.4b(1) allegation.
We also find res judicata and collateral estoppel do not bar
Leary’s UPC because the instant UPC concerns different claims
from the previous UPC. Additionally, we find that neither
Leary’s internal appeal to the State PBA nor his state lawsuit
against the Township give rise to issues of concurrent
jurisdiction that would conflict with the Commission’s
jurisdiction over his UPC against the PBA. Finally, we find that
Leary’s UPC is not moot because there remains an open issue with
practical significance (Leary’s pending suspension from the PBA),
there may be a continuing chilling effect from the PBA’s alleged
misconduct, and a cease and desist order may be necessary to
prevent future adverse action against Leary or other PBA members
who exercise their right under the Act to file a UPC against
their union. See Galloway Township Bd. of Ed., 78 N.J. 25
(1978); PBA Local 334 (Mendoza), supra; Salem Cty. Sheriff’s

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-42 10.
Dept., P.E.R.C. No. 2024-7, 50 NJPER 187 (¶41 2023); and Hudson
Cty., P.E.R.C. No. 2012-48, 38 NJPER 331 (¶111 2012).
ORDER
The unfair practice charge is remanded to the Director of
Unfair Practices for issuance of a Complaint.
BY ORDER OF THE COMMISSION

section 5.4a(7) or 5.4b(5), your allegations

No. 82-74, 8 NJPER 121 (¶13052 1982);
Palisades Park Bor., D.U.P. No. 78-1, 3 NJPER

Westfield, P.E.R.C. No. 90-32, 15 NJPER 618

Respondent's conduct does not satisfy our
pleading requirements. A charge should plead
with specificity the “who, what, when, where
and how” information about the commission of
an unfair practice in order to afford
Respondents adequate notice of the legal and
factual claims against them. State of New
Jersey (Judiciary), D.U.P. No. 2022-8, 48
NJPER 344 (¶77 2022); Edison Tp., D.U.P. No.
2012-9, 38 NJPER 269 (¶92 2012), aff’d

NJPER 287 (¶80 2017).

based upon what can be gleaned from your
charge “as is”, it is unclear who did what
AND when they did same. Accordingly, you have
failed to demonstrate that an alleged/viable
unfair practice may have been committed
within six months of when your original
charge was filed on January 14, 2026, and
therefore your allegations fall outside the
Commission's jurisdiction. Moreover, the
amended and second unfair practice charges

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 7.
fail to provide a sufficient basis to toll
the six-month statute of limitations

explanation regarding how/if you were

presumed to know the law.” State v. Moran,
202 N.J.311, 315, 319-320 (2010) (citing

(1833) (noting “a common maxim, familiar to
all minds, that ignorance of the law will not
excuse any person, either civilly or
criminally”)).

Cty. and Middlesex Council #7 (Mackaronis),

P.E.R.C. No. 81-62, 6 NJPER 555, 557 (¶11282
1981), aff’d App. Div. Docket No. A-1455-80.

of discretion the Commission will generally

processing and/or settlement of grievances.
State of New Jersey (JJC) and CWA Local 1040
(Thorpe), D.U.P. No. 2012-8, 38 NJPER 248
(¶83 2011), aff'd P.E.R.C. No. 2013-29, 39

not subsequently challenge the payroll

19:14-2.3(a), your charge is dismissed in its

of this action must be filed within 10 days

19:14-2.3(b).

D. The Parties’ Opposition to White’s Appeal.
On February 10, the Association filed its opposition to

substantive grounds. The Association contends that White’s
appeal is procedurally deficient because her “email filled with
external links” was not properly served nor did it meet the
requirements of a “self-contained document” set forth in N.J.A.C.
19:14-2.3(b). Further, the Association asserts that the “facts”
and attachments White included in her February 3 email appeal
5/ Under a section titled “Complete Record of Documents”, White
lists the 292 pages of attachments as follows: Original
Charge, “Ciripompa” Appellate Decision, PERC defect letter
dated January 27, 2026, Director’s Dismissal Order dated
January 22, 2026, My prior emails/appeal dated January 23-
24, 2026, Grievance emails to the Association from 2025,
Back-pay paystubs (“7 checks, Jan. 17, 2025"). White
states, “No other documents exist in the record.”
6/ White continued to send repetitive emails concerning her
appeal after February 3, 2026 that are not included as part
of the record.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 11.
were not previously presented prior to her appeal of the
Director’s decision, and therefore, must not be considered. The
Association asserts the Director’s decision properly found that
White’s January 16 UPC was beyond the 6-month statute of
limitations. The Association further argues that the Director’s
decision should be affirmed because she fails to plead any
specific facts that establish that the Association represented
her in a manner that was arbitrary, discriminatory, or in bad
faith. Further, the Association argues that White’s requested
relief is beyond the jurisdiction of the Commission. The
Association asserts that White’s claims asserting violations of
Title 18A are properly the jurisdiction of the Commissioner of
Education, her claims for improper unemployment or payroll
deductions are properly the jurisdiction of the Department of
Labor and Workforce Development, and her claims for improper
pension deductions are properly the jurisdiction of the Division
of Pensions.
On February 12, the Board filed its opposition to White’s
appeal of the Director’s decision. The Board asserts that White
has filed numerous complaints against the Board, regarding the
same allegations in the UPC, at the New Jersey Department of
Labor’s Wage and Hour Division and the New Jersey Department of
Education, and she has withdrawn each of the complaints. The
Board further argues the Director’s dismissal of the UPCs should

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 12.
be affirmed because the relief sought by the charges is outside
the authority of the Commission.
ANALYSIS
The Commission has authority to issue a complaint where it
appears that a charging party’s allegations, if true, may
constitute an unfair practice within the meaning of the Act.
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4c; N.J.A.C. 19:14-2.1. We affirm the
Director’s decision to dismiss White’s UPC because she did not
plead sufficient facts to support the alleged violations of the
Act.7/
I. Charges Against the Board
White’s N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4a(5) charge against the Board
alleges “discrimination in employment terms to discourage union
membership, via targeted over-deductions.” The Director found
that individual employees do not have standing to pursue such a
charge because the employer’s duty to negotiate in good faith
only runs to the majority representative. New Jersey Tpk. Auth.
v. Beall, 1981 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 9 (App. Div. 1981),
aff’g, P.E.R.C. No. 81-64, 6 NJPER 560 (¶11284 1980); Sussex Cty.
Sheriff’s Office, P.E.R.C. No. 2021-49, 47 NJPER 527 (¶123 2021);
and Essex Cty. (Miller), P.E.R.C. No. 2019-16, 45 NJPER 195 (¶50
2018). We agree with the Director.
7/ As a threshold issue, we agree with the Director that
White’s filings do not demonstrate that they were timely
filed.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 13.
Next, we turn to White’s N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4a(1) charge
against the Board, asserting its “interfer[ence] with union
rights by undermining NJEA dues and employee protections.”8/
White’s dispute against the Board stems from alleged improper
payroll deductions from a back pay award she obtained in a tenure
arbitration. In her February 3, 2026 appeal, she states, “I was
suspended on tenure charges; later, I obtained an
arbitration/back-pay award governed by N.J.S.A. 18A:6-14.”
(Emphasis added). In the attachments to her appeals, she
includes the tenure arbitrator’s award, which expressly states,
“I will retain jurisdiction of this matter to resolve any dispute
that arises as to the implementation of this award.” (Emphasis
added).
We agree with the Director that the record contains no
grounds for this agency to obtain jurisdiction over White’s
allegations concerning allegedly improper payroll deductions from
her back pay award. See State of New Jersey (Department of
Corrections and Youth Justice Commission, P.E.R.C. No. 2026-11,
52 NJPER 129 (¶33 2025)(dismissing an a(1) and (5) charge by an
individual employee against a public employer regarding disputed
pension calculations because this agency lacked jurisdiction over
such claims). Such jurisdiction may rest with the tenure
8/ We note that the January 21 second amended charge excludes
the a(3) charge which was raised in the January 16 amended
charge.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 14.
arbitrator, the Commissioner of Education9/, the Department of
Labor and/or the Division of Pensions and Benefits.10/ Thus, the
Director correctly dismissed the N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4a(1) charge
against the Board.
III. Charge Against the Association
We next address White’s appeal of the Director’s dismissal
of her N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4b(1) charge against the Association,
alleging that it failed to file proposed grievances and ignored
her requests for assistance with the allegedly improper payroll
deductions.
In White’s January 16, 2026 first amended charge she states:
Beginning in 2025 and continuing thereafter,
I repeatedly sought assistance from my unions
(NJEA and EEA) regarding the improper
deduction and the Board’s refusal to correct
it. I filed grievances and sent multiple
emails, letters, and demands for action to
the NJEA/EEA and its assigned counsel . . . .
to no avail.
In White’s January 21 second amended charge she states that the
Association “[failed] to comply with grievance procedures or CBA
terms on payroll.”
9/ Pursuant to N.J.S.A. 18A:6-9, the Commissioner of Education
“shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine, without cost
to the parties, all controversies and disputes arising under
the school laws...”
10/ The Board asserts that White had complaints pending in other
venues but withdrew those complaints.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 15.
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4b(1) prohibits an employee organization
from “interfering with, restraining, or coercing employees in the
exercise of the rights guaranteed to them by the Act.” A breach
of the duty of fair representation violates subsection 5.4b(1) of
the Act and occurs when a union’s conduct towards a member of the
negotiations unit is arbitrary, discriminatory or in bad faith.
Lullo v. IAFF, 55 N.J. 409 (1970); D’Arrigo v. New Jersey State
Bd. of Mediation, 119 N.J. 74, 76 (1990); Belen v. Woodbridge Tp.
Bd. of Ed., 142 N.J. Super. 486 (App. Div. 1976); see also Vaca
v. Sipes, 386 U.S. 171 (1967).
A review of White’s emails about the alleged improper
payroll deductions demonstrates that they were largely directed
to the Board and its counsel, with multiple people copied
including Association representatives. The emails suggest that
White and the Board were involved in an appeal over payroll
deductions before the Department of Labor, and that she asked the
Association to provide her with different representation and
pursue grievances on her behalf.
The duty of fair representation does not require a union to
arbitrate every grievance. Essex Cty. (Miller), P.E.R.C. No.
2019-16, 45 NJPER 195 (¶50 2018); Passaic Cty. Support Staff
Ass’n, P.E.R.C. No. 2015-23, 41 NJPER 169 (¶60 2014). Unions are
provided wide latitude in determining whether a grievance is
meritorious and warrants action.11/ White’s emails show that the
11/ The Commission has frequently dismissed claims alleging that
(continued...)

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-41 16.
Association was on notice of both the Department of Labor appeal
and White’s dissatisfaction with her union representation.
However, given the discretion afforded unions in deciding whether
a grievance is meritorious, the emails do not establish that the
Association represented her in a manner that was arbitrary,
discriminatory or in bad faith. See Lullo v. IAFF, supra.
Thus, we affirm the Director’s decision dismissing White’s
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4b(1) charge.
For all the foregoing reasons, we sustain the Director’s
January 22, 2026 decision dismissing White’s UPCs in their
entirety.
ORDER
The Charging Party’s appeal of the Director’s January 22,
2026 decision is denied.
BY ORDER OF THE COMMISSION
Chair Hennessy-Shotter, Commissioners Davey, Higgins, Hines, and
Papero voted in favor of this decision. None opposed.
Commissioner Eaton was not present.

Trenton, New Jersey

violated the duty of fair representation. See, e.g., Essex

(¶23043 1992); AFSCME, Co. 52, Loc. 888 (Brennan), P.E.R.C.
No. 89-71, 15 NJPER 71 (¶20027 1988); Camden Cty. College
(Porreca), P.E.R.C. No. 88-28, 13 NJPER 755 (¶18285 1987);
