text:
P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-40
STATE OF NEW JERSEY
BEFORE THE PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS COMMISSION
In the Matter of
SOUTH ORANGE-MAPLEWOOD BOARD
OF EDUCATION,
Petitioner,
-and- Docket No. SN-2026-018
SOUTH ORANGE-MAPLEWOOD EDUCATION
ASSOCIATION,
Respondent.
SYNOPSIS
The Public Employment Relations Commission grants in part,
and denies in part, the Board’s petition to restrain binding
arbitration of three grievances filed by the Association. The
Association’s grievances contest the Board’s scheduling of
professional development (PD) days prior to September, as well as
the total number of PD days scheduled and the dates on which
those PD days are scheduled during the 2025-2026 school year.
The Commission finds that the grievances are not legally
arbitrable to the extent they challenge the Board’s decision to
schedule a PD day in September prior to the start of the student
school year, as it would infringe on the Board’s managerial
prerogative to determine the student calendar. However, the
Commission finds that the specific date selected for the pre-
school-year PD is legally arbitrable. The Commission also finds
that, in the absence of an articulated dominant educational
policy reason for allegedly increasing the number of PD days, the
total number of PD days scheduled, as well as when they are
scheduled during the student school year, is legally arbitrable.
This synopsis is not part of the Commission decision. It
has been prepared for the convenience of the reader. It has been
neither reviewed nor approved by the Commission.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-40
STATE OF NEW JERSEY
BEFORE THE PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS COMMISSION
In the Matter of
SOUTH ORANGE-MAPLEWOOD BOARD
OF EDUCATION,
Petitioner,
-and- Docket No. SN-2026-018
SOUTH ORANGE-MAPLEWOOD EDUCATION
ASSOCIATION,
Respondent.
Appearances:
For the Petitioner, Lenox, Socey, Formidoni, Giordano,
Carrigg, Lang & Casey, LLC, attorneys (Patrick F.
Carrigg, of counsel; Victoria R. Lang, on the brief)
For the Respondent, Selikoff & Cohen, P.A., attorneys
(Keith Waldman, of counsel and on the brief; Liz Pudel,
on the brief)
DECISION
On November 19, 2025, the South Orange-Maplewood Board of
Education (Board) filed a scope of negotiations petition seeking
a restraint of binding arbitration of three grievances filed by
the South Orange-Maplewood Education Association (Association or
SOMEA). The grievances assert that the Board violated the
parties’ collective negotiations agreement (CNA) by scheduling a
faculty-only professional development (PD) day prior to
September. The grievances also contest the total number of PD
days, as well as the dates on which those days were scheduled for
the 2025-2026 school year.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-40 2.
The Board filed briefs, exhibits, and the certification of
its Superintendent. The Association filed a brief and the
certification of its Chairperson for the Professional Rights and
Responsibilities Committee. These facts appear.
The Association represents certified teaching staff members
and non-certified support staff members. The Board and
Association are parties to a CNA with a term of July 1, 2021
through June 30, 2024. The grievance procedure ends in binding
arbitration.
Article XX of the CNA is entitled “Employee Work Year.”
Article XX.A. provides the “in-school work year for teachers on a
ten (10) month basis” as consisting of:
• “One hundred-eight three (183) days which pupils are in
attendance”;
• “One (1) additional day for fall orientation program”;
• “One (1) day for closing school following the last day of
pupil attendance”;
• “Two (2) days for the professional development of teachers
to be scheduled during the course of the instructional
year”;
• “A total of four (4) days for orientation of new teachers
prior to school opening”; and
• “full days for teachers” on “The last two (2) student days
in June.”
Article XX.C.1. of the CNA provides: “All supportive
employees on a ten (10) or eleven (11) month schedule should
report for work on September 1st or the day after Labor Day,

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-40 3.
whichever is earlier.” Article XXI.A.6.e.3. references “the
start of school in September” regarding when high school teachers
must have evening activity calendars ready. Article XXI.D.1.a.
of the CNA refers to the “Regular Work Day” for secretaries as
occurring from “September 1st - June 30th.”
The Superintendent certifies that on or about February 27,
2025, the Board approved the school calendar for the 2025-2026
school year. The approved calendar established two PD days, on
Wednesday, August 27 and Thursday, August 28, 2025, followed by a
4-day Labor Day weekend and then the first day of school for
students on September 2, 2025.1/ The calendar also established
PD half days on October 14, 2025, November 4, 2025, January 13,
2026, February 24, 2026, and April 14, 2026.
On August 15, 2025, the Association submitted a Level III
grievance to the Superintendent asserting that the 2025-2026
school calendar violates the CNA by establishing August 27, 2025
as the first day for teachers to report for PD. As a remedy, the
grievance sought a new school calendar in which teachers’ first
workday occurs in September, compensation for attendance on
August 27 and 28, 2025, and any other make whole remedies.
On August 25, the Superintendent e-mailed the Association
President a grievance response that partially sustained the
1/ The calendar also included four earlier “New Staff
Orientation” days scheduled for August 20, 21, 25, and 26
that the Association’s grievances do not dispute.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-40 4.
grievance by making the second pre-student school year PD day
(Thursday, August 28) “a nonmandatory day for staff to work on
their classrooms” while maintaining the mandatory PD day
scheduled for Wednesday, August 27.
On or about August 27, 2025, the Association elevated three
Level IV grievances, one entitled “Teacher Start Date Violation”
concerning the start of the teacher work year prior to September,
one entitled “Professional Development Violation” alleging that
the number of PD days scheduled for the 2025-2026 school year is
contractually prohibited, and one entitled “Work Year Violation
(11-Month Employees)” asserting that on August 13, 2025 the Board
violated Article XX.C. of the CNA when it advised 11-month
employees that they needed to report to work ten days prior to
the start of the student school year.
On September 25, 2025, the Board denied all three
Association grievances, followed by explanations of the denials
on October 3. The Board’s counsel stated that the Association’s
grievance seeking to prevent the work year from starting before
September interferes with the Board’s prerogative to establish
the school calendar.2/ He further stated that “Professional
development during teacher orientation and on half days
2/ The Board’s counsel did not specifically distinguish between
the “Teacher Start Date Violation” grievance and the “Work
Year Violation (11-Month Employees)” grievance, both of
which alleged CNA violations for working prior to September.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-40 5.
throughout the school year is consistent with past practice” and
that the Superintendent had granted the Association’s request for
August 28, 2025 to be an optional day. On November 12, the
Association filed a Request for Submission of a Panel of
Arbitrators. This petition ensued.
Local 195, IFPTE v. State, 88 N.J. 393 (1982), articulates
the standards for determining whether a subject is mandatorily
negotiable:
[A] subject is negotiable between public
employers and employees when (1) the item
intimately and directly affects the work and
welfare of public employees; (2) the subject
has not been fully or partially preempted by
statute or regulation; and (3) a negotiated
agreement would not significantly interfere
with the determination of governmental
policy. To decide whether a negotiated
agreement would significantly interfere with
the determination of governmental policy, it
is necessary to balance the interests of the
public employees and the public employer.
When the dominant concern is the government’s
managerial prerogative to determine policy, a
subject may not be included in collective
negotiations even though it may intimately
affect employees’ working conditions.
[Id. at 404-405].
“Questions concerning whether subjects are mandatorily negotiable
should be made on a case-by-case basis.” Troy v. Rutgers, 168
N.J. 354, 383 (2001). We must balance the parties’ interests in
light of the particular facts and arguments presented. City of
Jersey City v. Jersey City POBA, 154 N.J. 555, 574-575 (1998).

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-40 6.
The Commission’s inquiry on a scope of negotiations petition
is quite narrow. We are addressing a single issue in the
abstract: whether the subject matter in dispute is within the
scope of collective negotiations. The merits of the
Association’s claimed violation of the agreement, as well as the
Board’s contractual defenses, are not in issue, because those are
matters for the arbitrator to decide if the Commission determines
that the question is one that may be arbitrated. Ridgefield Park
Ed. Ass’n v. Ridgefield Park Bd. of Ed., 78 N.J. 144, 154 (1978).
The Board asserts that the Association’s grievance is not
arbitrable because the establishment of the school calendar is a
non-negotiable managerial prerogative. It argues that its
decision to schedule PD days prior to the start of the school
year as well as on half days during the school year is not
negotiable. The Board contends that because its scheduling of
the PD days did not exceed the student calendar, there was no
unilateral change in a negotiable term of employment.
The Association asserts that its grievances are arbitrable
because they concern the scheduling of the parts of the employee
work year when students are not in school. It argues that the
Board’s imposition of PD days goes beyond those set forth in the
CNA and that the scheduling of PD days on half days when students
are no longer present is a negotiable scheduling issue. The

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-40 7.
Association contends that the issue of compensation for hours
worked in excess of the negotiated work year is arbitrable.
N.J.S.A. 18A:36-1 provides that the “school year” for public
schools “shall begin on July 1 and end on June 30.” Within that
school year, a board of education “shall determine annually the
dates, between which the schools of the district shall be open,
in accordance with law.” N.J.S.A. 18A:36-2. It is well-
established that the determination of a school calendar in terms
of when school commences and terminates is a non-negotiable
managerial prerogative. Woodstown-Pilesgrove Reg. H.S. Bd. of
Ed., 81 N.J. 582, 592 (1980); and Piscataway Tp. Bd. of Ed., 307
N.J. Super. 263, 270 (App. Div. 1998).
However, the Commission and courts have recognized the
distinction between the student calendar and faculty work
schedules, noting that faculty work schedules are mandatorily
negotiable to the extent negotiations do not interfere with
scheduling the student school year. Burlington Cty. College
Faculty Ass’n, 64 N.J. 10, 12 (1973); Troy v. Rutgers, 168 N.J.
at 383; and N.J.I.T., 1980 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 20, NJPER
Supp.2d 263 (¶218 App. Div. 1980), aff’g P.E.R.C. No. 80-54, 5
NJPER 491, 493 (¶10251 1979). Thus, although there is nearly
complete overlap between the student school year and faculty work
year, “once the overall school calendar and the student days are
established, negotiations over the timing and placement of non-

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-40 8.
student faculty work days within that school calendar are
mandatorily negotiable unless a board can demonstrate that it
would significantly interfere with educational policy goals.”
Southampton Tp. Bd. of Ed., 2020 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 1020,
46 NJPER 555 (¶126 App. Div. 2020), aff’g P.E.R.C. No. 2019-41,
45 NJPER 372, 376 (¶97 2019) (Southampton I).
The Association’s grievances seek to arbitrate the following
issues:
1) The faculty-only mandatory PD day scheduled for Wednesday,
August 27, 2025, prior to the start of the student school
year;
2) the total number of PD days for the 2025-2026 school year;
and
3) the scheduling of the remaining PD days during the 2025-2026
school year.
We first address the negotiability of the faculty-only PD
day scheduled for August 27, 2025. The student school year was
scheduled to begin on September 2, the day after Labor Day. The
Association seeks to move the faculty-only PD day into September.
However, because of the way the calendar fell that year,
scheduling the PD day in September would either conflict with the
beginning of the student school year or eliminate the Board’s
ability to hold a PD day before students returned.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-40 9.
The scheduling of faculty-only work days is non-negotiable
to the extent negotiations would interfere with a board’s
prerogative to determine the start of the student school year.
See Southampton Tp. Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 2021-37, 47 NJPER
409, 412 (¶97 2021) (Southampton II) (scheduling of non-student
faculty work days was non-negotiable to the extent it would
change the Board’s prerogative to start the student school year
immediately after Labor Day); see also Bethlehem Tp. Bd. of Ed.,
2015 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 1944, 42 NJPER 71 (¶18 App. Div.
2015), aff’g P.E.R.C. No. 2014-47, 40 NJPER 337 (¶123 2014)
(change in faculty start date to August to begin one day prior to
start of student school year that was shifted to align with
regional high school was non-negotiable); W. Morris Reg’l High
Sch. Bd. of Ed., 2018 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 1993, 45 NJPER 89
(¶23 App. Div. 2018), aff’g P.E.R.C. No. 2017-29, 43 NJPER 225
(¶68 2016) (proposal to set faculty work year between September 1
and June 30 was non-negotiable because it would preclude Board
from scheduling the student school year beyond those dates); and
Essex Fells Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 2018-2, 44 NJPER 71 (¶22
2017) (change in faculty start date to August to accommodate
shift in student start date prior to Labor Day to align with
regional district was not negotiable). Accordingly, the
Association’s grievances are not legally arbitrable to the extent
they challenge the Board’s decision to schedule a PD day prior to

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-40 10.
the start of the student school year. However, the specific date
selected for that pre-school-year PD is legally arbitrable.
Belvidere Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 78-62, 4 NJPER 165, 166 (¶4080
1978), aff’d, 1979 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 12, NJPER Supp.2d 57
(¶37 App. Div. 1979); Edison Tp. Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 78-53,
4 NJPER 151, 152 (¶4070 1978); see also Southampton I, aff’d,
Southampton I (App. Div.) (board committed unfair practice by
refusing to negotiate over the scheduling of two staff
development days for times that would not interfere with the
student calendar); and Southampton II (negotiations over the
timing of two staff development days during the week before the
start of the student school year did not significantly interfere
with determination of education policy).
We turn next to the negotiability of the total number of PD
days for the 2025-2026 school year, as well as when the remaining
PD days were scheduled during the student school year. The
record does not contain a specific rationale for the Board’s
asserted managerial prerogative for allegedly increasing the
total number of PD days or for scheduling those PD days on the
dates they were scheduled. In the absence of specific rationale
supporting the Board’s asserted managerial prerogative, we find
the total number of PD days scheduled, as well as the scheduling
of the remaining PD days during the student school year, to be

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-40 11.
legally arbitrable. Belvidere Bd. of Ed., supra; Edison Tp. Bd.
of Ed., supra; see also Southampton I, supra.
This case is distinguishable from Franklin Lakes Bd. of Ed.,
P.E.R.C. No. 2018-44, 44 NJPER 407 (¶113 2018), relied on by the
Board, in which the Commission restrained arbitration over the
scheduling of a professional development day, but allowed
arbitration over additional compensation for the alleged workload
increase. There, it was undisputed that the number of faculty-
only work days was unchanged where the board rescheduled an end-
of-year “pack and clean” day to instead be an additional staff
training day prior to the start of the school year. The record
in Franklin Lakes demonstrated a dominant educational policy
reason for the change in the scheduling and type of non-student
faculty work day, supported by the superintendent’s certification
that the change was made “to ensure that adequate time was
available to provide necessary training to staff members for the
successful opening of the 2017-2018 school year.” As discussed
above, the record here does not provide an explanation of the
Board’s asserted managerial prerogative regarding the total
number of PD days for the 2025-2026 school year or for the
scheduling of the PD days that took place during the student
school year.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-40 12.
ORDER
The South Orange-Maplewood Board of Education’s request for
a restraint of binding arbitration of the Associations’s August
27 PD grievance is granted to the extent the grievance challenges
the Board’s decision to schedule a faculty-only PD day prior to
the start of the student school year. The request is denied to
the extent the grievance contests the specific date selected for
the faculty-only PD prior to the start of the student school
year.
The Board’s request for a restraint of binding arbitration
of the Association’s grievance challenging the total number of PD
days for the 2025-2026 school year, as well as the dates on which
the remaining PD days were scheduled during the student school
year, is denied.
BY ORDER OF THE COMMISSION
Chair Hennessy-Shotter, Commissioners Davey, Higgins, Hines, and
Papero voted in favor of this decision. None opposed.
Commissioner Eaton was not present.
ISSUED: May 28, 2026
Trenton, New Jersey

text:
P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-39
STATE OF NEW JERSEY
BEFORE THE PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS COMMISSION
In the Matter of
CAMDEN COUNTY JUDICIARY and
OPEIU, LOCAL 32
Respondents,
-and- Docket No. CI-2026-027
SYLVIA COLE,
Charging Party.
SYNOPSIS
The Public Employment Relations Commission denies Sylvia
Cole’s appeal of the dismissal of an unfair practice charge filed
against her former employer, Camden County Judiciary, and her
majority representative, OPEIU, Local 21. Cole alleges that the
Judiciary retaliated against her for protected activity under the
Act and interfered with those rights when it imposed discipline
against her. She also alleges that OPEIU breached its duty of
fair representation when it did not process a grievance for a 2-
day suspension. The Commission affirms the Director of Unfair
Practices’ dismissal of the charge, finding: (1) that the UPC did
not establish that the Judiciary knew she engaged in protected
activity and that disciplinary disputes are generally not
reviewed by the Commission and (2) OPEIU’s initial delay and
subsequent decision not to file a grievance over a 2-day
suspension for a former employee was not a breach of the duty of
fair representation.

This appeal followed. Cole only appeals the 5.4b(1)
allegation against OPEIU. Although she asserts the Judiciary
committed unfair practices, she did not specify which allegations
she seeks to be reviewed. Because she did not assert that a PERC
rule or regulation was violated, we treat her appeal as limited
to claims under subsections 5.4a(1) and 5.4a(3). Cole filed a
letter brief and exhibits. The Judiciary filed a brief in
opposition. OPEIU was served on January 29, 2026 but did not
file a response.
Cole argues that a complaint should have been issued against
OPEIU because it breached its duty of fair representation when it
did not appeal her suspension due to a missed email. Cole also
contends that the Judiciary committed an unfair practice by
improperly disciplining her, failing to conduct a proper
investigation, and violating the CNA.
The Judiciary argues that it does not owe Cole a duty of
fair representation and that her contractual claims fall outside
the Commission’s unfair practice jurisdiction.
The Commission has authority to issue a complaint where it
appears that a charging party’s allegations, if true, may
constitute an unfair practice within the meaning of the Act.
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4c; N.J.A.C. 19:14-2.1. The issue is whether

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-39 6.
Cole alleged sufficient facts, that, if true, would constitute a
breach of OPEIU’s duty of fair representation and whether the
Judiciary engaged in conduct constituting an unfair practice. We
affirm the Director’s dismissal.
(a) Claims against the Judiciary
Cole’s retaliation claim under subsection 5.4a(3) was
properly dismissed.
Protected activity includes conduct in connection with
collective negotiations, grievance processing, contract
interpretation or administration, or other related activity on
behalf of a union or individual. North Brunswick Bd. of Educ. v.
North Brunswick Educ. Sec’ys Ass’n, 1979 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS
13 (App. Div. 1979), aff’g P.E.R.C. No. 79-14, 4 NJPER 451 (¶4205
1978). While Cole requested that OPEIU file a grievance, there
is no allegation that the Judiciary was aware of that intent. In
fact, the UPC alleges that her employer had not received any
filing related to the grievance.
We further find the amended UPC does not establish the
necessary elements supporting Cole’s claim that the Judiciary
interfered with her rights under the Act. A public employer
violates section 5.4a(1) of the Act if its action tends to
interfere with an employee’s statutory rights and lacks a
legitimate and substantial business justification. Mine Hill
Tp., P.E.R.C. No. 86-145, 12 NJPER 526 (¶17197 1986); NJ Sports &

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-39 7.
Exposition Auth., P.E.R.C. No. 80-73, 5 NJPER 550 (¶10285 1979).
Cole alleges that the Judiciary improperly investigated her
conduct and suspended her in violation of the CNA—then caused her
constructive discharge from employment. This Commission, in
general, does not review disciplinary actions, and Cole’s
discipline, both the two-day suspension and the alleged
constructive discharge, were subject to review through the
parties’ negotiated disciplinary procedures. See, e.g., State of
New Jersey, (Kearney), P.E.R.C. No. 2025-19, 51 NJPER 175 (¶44
2024). Thus, we affirm the Director’s dismissal of these claims.
(b) Claims against OPEIU
The amended UPC does not establish that OPEIU breached its
duty of fair representation.
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4b(1) prohibits an employee organization
from “interfering with, restraining, or coercing employees in the
exercise of the rights guaranteed to them by the Act.” An
employee organization violates this proscription when its action
tends to interfere with protected rights and lacks a legitimate
and substantial organizational justification. FOP, Lodge No. 12
(Colisanti), P.E.R.C. No. 90-65, 16 NJPER 126 (¶21049 1990).
Section 5.3 of the Act empowers a union to negotiate
collectively and administer the CNA on behalf of all unit
employees. With that exclusive authority comes the duty to
fairly represent all unit employees in negotiations and contract

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-39 8.
administration. A breach of the duty of fair representation
occurs when a union’s conduct towards a member of the
negotiations unit is arbitrary, discriminatory or in bad faith.
Lullo v. IAFF, 55 N.J. 409 (1970); D’Arrigo v. New Jersey State
Bd. of Mediation, 119 N.J. 74, 76 (1990); Belen v. Woodbridge Tp.
Bd. of Ed., 142 N.J. Super. 486 (App. Div. 1976); see also Vaca
v. Sipes, 386 U.S. 171 (1967). “The complete satisfaction of all
who are represented is hardly to be expected” and “[a] wide range
of reasonableness must be allowed a statutory bargaining
representative in servicing the unit it represents, subject
always to complete good faith and honesty of purpose in the
exercise of its discretion.” PBA Local 187, P.E.R.C. No. 2005-
78, 31 NJPER 173 (¶70 2005) (citing Ford Motor Co. v. Huffman,
345 U.S. 330, 337-338 (1953)). A breach of the duty of fair
representation violates subsection 5.4b(1) of the Act.
While “[a] union must exercise reasonable care and diligence
in investigating, processing, and presenting grievances; and must
evaluate the merits of requests for arbitration in good faith,”
“[p]roof of union negligence, poor judgment, or even ineptitude,
standing alone, does not suffice to prove a breach of the duty of
fair representation.” State of New Jersey Judiciary
(Administrative Office of the Courts), P.E.R.C. No. 2026-9, 52
NJPER 100 (¶25 2025) (citations omitted); N.J. Turnpike Auth.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-39 9.
(Papajani), P.E.R.C. No. 2022-38, 48 NJPER 393 (¶90 2022)
(citations omitted).
Here, Cole alleges in the amended UPC, and provides
documentary evidence on appeal, that her OPEIU representative
sent an email to OPEIU President Short, informing her that Cole
wished to appeal her two-day suspension. Cole also alleges that
Short was negligent when she missed the email and never took
action in processing the appeal, even after Cole personally
informed her of the missed email and reiterated her request to
contest her suspension.
Short’s initial inaction in filing a grievance after missing
an email related to minor discipline was “mere negligence” that,
alone, does not rise to an unfair practice. Short’s further
inaction on the grievance once personally notified of Cole’s
desire to contest her two-day suspension was also not an unfair
practice where Cole was already a former employee, having
resigned relatively quickly after being served with the two-day
suspension. Thus, it was not arbitrary, capricious, or in bad
faith for OPEIU to decline to process the grievance for a 2-day
suspension for a resigned member where the time and costs of
challenging the suspension would outweigh the available relief to
Cole. The Director’s dismissal of this charge is affirmed.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-39 10.
ORDER
The Director’s letter dismissal of the amended UPC is
affirmed.

SYNOPSIS
The Public Employment Relations Commission denies the
Atlantic County Prosecutor’s Office’s (ACPO) motion to dismiss
the SOA’s Petition to Initiate Compulsory Interest Arbitration
(IA petition). The Commission finds that, pursuant to N.J.S.A.
34:13A-16b(2) and N.J.A.C. 19:16-5.2(a)(1)-(2), either party may
file an IA petition on after the date the collective negotiations
agreement (CNA) expires. Therefore, the Commission finds that
failure of the parties to comply with the Act’s requirement to
commence negotiations at least 120 days prior to contract
expiration does not preclude the filing of an IA petition after
CNA expiration. The Commission further finds that unfair
practice proceedings are the mechanism for addressing alleged
refusals to negotiate prior to contract expiration, but do not
operate as a bar to filing an IA petition upon CNA expiration.

LLC, attorneys (Christopher A. Gray, Esq., of counsel)
DECISION
On February 2, 2026, Mainland PBA, Local 77 (SOA) filed a
Petition to Initiate Compulsory Interest Arbitration (IA) for a
successor collective negotiations agreement (CNA) with the
Atlantic County Prosecutor’s Office (ACPO).1/ On February 26,
the ACPO filed an unfair practice charge seeking to restrain the
1/ We take administrative notice that on February 2, 2026, PBA
Local 77 (Rank and File Detectives) and PBA Local 77
(Detective Sergeants) also filed IA petitions indicating
those CNAs also expired on December 31, 2025. Docket Nos.
IA-2026-13 and -14. These petitions indicate three (3)
negotiation dates.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-38 2.
IA process.2/ On March 13, the ACPO filed a motion to dismiss
the SOA’s petition.3/ On March 20, the SOA filed a brief
opposing the motion and a cross-motion for costs and fees. On
April 2, the ACPO sought leave to file a reply brief, which was
granted with an opportunity for the SOA to file a sur-reply. On
April 6, the ACPO filed its reply, and on April 7, the SOA filed
its sur-reply. The following facts appear.
The SOA represents a unit of nine (9) Detective Lieutenants
and Detective Captains. The IA petition states that the parties’
CNA expired on December 31, 2025, and reflects that no
negotiation sessions were held prior to expiration. The petition
identifies the following economic issues in dispute: salary,
overtime, on-call compensation, call-in pay, and commander
compensation.
The ACPO seeks dismissal of the IA petition, asserting that
the parties have not engaged in three (3) negotiation sessions
prior to the SOA’s filing for IA. It contends that the IA
statute requires at least three sessions before invoking IA and
that this requirement applies regardless of when the petition is
filed. According to ACPO, the SOA’s filing violates the IA Act
2/ The ACPO’s charge, Docket No. CE-2026-007, is being procesed
in the normal course.
3/ ACPO also filed a motion to dismiss IA-2026-14 that it
subsequently withdrew as the parties successfully reached a
successor CNA during the interest arbitration process.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-38 3.
and is inconsistent with precedent requiring a good-faith effort
to negotiate before invoking IA. The ACPO further argues that
Commission regulations permitting filing upon contract expiration
do not eliminate the three-session requirement or authorize
parties to bypass negotiations entirely.
The SOA responds that, although the parties did not meet
before the contract expired, Commission rules expressly permit
either party to file for IA after expiration. It further asserts
that the ACPO never sought to initiate negotiations prior to
expiration. The SOA also argues that the ACPO’s motion was filed
38 days after the petition, which is beyond the statutory
five-day period to file an answer, and that the ACPO cannot
establish a refusal to negotiate where it never demanded
negotiations as required by the Act.
The SOA additionally notes that, following the filing of its
petition, the parties participated in mediation sessions and
contends that dismissal would delay the statutorily streamlined
IA process. It seeks costs and fees, asserting that the ACPO did
not satisfy pre-IA statutory and regulatory requirements and has
not demonstrated bad faith on its part.
The ACPO replies that the SOA overstates the extent of
mediation, asserting that only one and one-half days of mediation
occurred and those sessions would not have taken place had the
petition been rejected. It further contends that the SOA’s

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-38 4.
timeliness arguments are misplaced because the cited regulations
apply to unfair practice charges filed prior to CNA expiration
and do not govern motion practice. The ACPO maintains that it
did not cause a delay and that it acted diligently upon the
arbitrator’s assignment. It also opposes the request for fees,
arguing that N.J.A.C. 19:16-5.2(b) applies only to pre-expiration
unfair practice charges, not post-expiration proceedings.
The SOA responds that the ACPO has neither demonstrated a
refusal to negotiate nor filed a Notice of Intent to Commence
Negotiations, and to date, has not requested negotiations.
ANALYSIS
The Police and Fire Public Interest Arbitration Reform Act
(Reform Act), P.L. 1995, c. 425, as amended, is codified at
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-14 through -21. The Act requires public
employers and exclusive representatives of police and fire units
to commence negotiations at least 120 days prior to CNA
expiration. If negotiations reach an impasse, either party may
request mediation. N.J.S.A. 34:13A-16a. If the impasse
persists, either party may request that the Commission “invoke
factfinding with recommendation for settlement of all issues in
dispute.” N.J.S.A. 34:13A-16b(1). The statute further provides
that, “[r]egardless of the mediation and factfinding procedures,”
either party may petition for IA on or after the date the CNA
expires. N.J.S.A. 34:13A-16b(2). Commission regulations likewise

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-38 5.
permit the filing of an IA petition upon contract expiration.
N.J.A.C. 19:16-5.2(a)(1)-(2).
The Act requires parties to negotiate in good faith prior to
invoking impasse procedures. However, neither the Act nor the
Commission’s regulations state that failure to so precludes
either party from filing an IA petition. N.J.A.C. 19:16-5.2(a)
permits filing an IA petition on or after CNA expiration and does
not impose a condition precedent of three negotiation sessions.
We decline to read such a requirement into the statute.
This interpretation is consistent with longstanding
Commission practice. The Division of Conciliation and
Arbitration processes IA petitions filed upon contract expiration
without requiring a threshold showing that a specified number of
negotiation sessions occurred. The structure of the Act also
supports this approach. It provides a mechanism - through unfair
practice proceedings - to address alleged refusals to negotiate
prior to CNA expiration, while separately authorizing IA upon
expiration. Read together, these provisions establish a
sequential framework for enforcing negotiation obligations and
resolving impasse, rather than one in which pre-expiration
conduct operates as a bar to filing an IA petition upon CNA
expiration. The ACPO did not avail itself of the pre-expiration
process and cannot rely on that omission to defeat the petition.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-38 6.
The ACPO’s reliance on City of Newark and Newark
Identification Officers Ass’n, P.E.R.C. No. 2006-84, 32 NJPER 159
(¶71 2006), is misplaced. In Newark, the association sought to
initiate IA, asserting that its prior CNA had expired in 2000.
The city moved to dismiss, contending that the parties had
negotiated and ratified a successor CNA extending through 2008.
The record showed that, in 2004, the parties reached agreement on
salary and benefits, and the association’s president executed a
memorandum incorporating those terms while continuing the
remaining provisions of the prior CNA. The Commission found that
the association ratified the agreement, that the city reasonably
relied on that ratification, and that the parties thereafter
operated under its terms. Concluding that a valid CNA remained
in effect and that the parties were not at impasse, the
Commission dismissed the IA petition. Although the decision
referenced the Act’s pre-expiration three-meeting requirement,
that mention was not essential to the holding and did not
establish a prerequisite filing requirement.
Here, the IA petition was properly filed upon CNA expiration
pursuant to N.J.A.C. 19:16-5.2(a). While parties are encouraged
to avail themselves of the Act’s and IA regulation’s mechanisms
for negotiations prior to CNA expiration, it is undisputed that
neither party took advantage of those opportunities. Both
parties therefore forwent the opportunity to pursue pre-

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-38 7.
expiration unfair practice remedies. It is for this reason that
we deny the SOA’s request for costs and fees. N.J.A.C.
19:16-5.2(b)(2) applies only where a party prevails on an unfair
practice charge alleging a refusal to negotiate filed prior to
CNA expiration. See, e.g., City of Newark and Newark Police SOA,
P.E.R.C. No. 2025-17, 51 NJPER 169 (¶42 2024)(granting summary
judgment to the SOA on a refusal to negotiate claim arising
within 120 days prior to CNA expiration, but denying costs and
fees where both parties did not strictly comply with the
applicable statutory and regulatory negotiation requirements).
Under these circumstances, we decline to construe the Act as
imposing a mandatory precondition requiring dismissal of a
petition filed upon CNA expiration.
ORDER
The ACPO’s motion to dismiss the interest arbitration
petition is denied.

Hines voted in favor of this decision. None opposed.

business justification. Finally, the Commission finds no basis

As amended, the UPC states that on the present record the

only the SOA’s amended 5.4a(1) and (5) claims:
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4a(1)
(interference/coercion):
an official written accusation of
criminality/illegality/moral turpitude
against the union's designee and President,
disseminated to counsel, the City Law
Director, and a subordinate unit member
(Captain [J.S.]), which objectively tends to
interfere with protected rights and lacks any
legitimate and substantial business
justification;
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4a(5)

after an admitted verbal demand to negotiate
over stipends/differentials and related
successor terms, the City refused to bargain

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 4.
and contaminated the bargaining channel by
criminalizing protected negotiations and
bypassing lawful labor processes (including
scope mechanisms).
In support of its motion for reconsideration and its
response to the defect letter, the SOA filed a brief, exhibits,
the supplemental certification of President J.W., and the
certification of Captain J.S., an SOA member who serves as the
Police Director’s Chief of Staff. The Commission received no
responsive filing from the City. These facts appear.
J.W. certifies that the parties are in negotiations for a
successor to their most recent collective negotiations agreement
(CNA) governing superior officers’ terms and conditions of
employment that expired on December 31, 2023. That CNA includes
a 4% compensation differential commonly referred to, J.W.
certifies, as “detective pay” or the “detective differential.”
He further certifies that this differential has been applied in
practice to certain atypical investigative or confidential
assignments, where the assignment is not a traditional case-

J.W. certifies that in October of 2024 the SOA submitted a

in lieu of a detective differential. In 2025, J.W. pursued
“administrative discussions” with various City representatives
(including the Mayor, the Mayor’s Chief of Staff, and the

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 5.
Business Administrator) about the proposed SOA President stipend
as well as a separate proposal for a stipend for the title of
Public Information Officer (PIO), which was also based on “the
existing detective differential framework.” J.W. certifies that
he followed up on these discussions relating to the stipend

The Police Director’s email that is the subject of this
dispute recounts a meeting that took place in his office on
November 7, 2025, when J.W. arrived, according to the email, “to
have a conversation” about “the contract situation between the
city and the unions (PBA & SOA)”. Dated November 13, the email
was sent to legal counsel for both the SOA and the City as well
as to President J.W. and Captain J.S., among others. It states

President [J.W.] then advised me that he felt
I should give him detective pay and expressed
the reasons why. I initially scoffed at the
idea but agreed I would hear him out. I
advised him that detective pay was only given
because one was doing detective work or one
was assigned to the Director’s Office. He
didn’t agree, offering different reasons that
are outside of the contract or past practice

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 6.
for awarding detective pay. President [J.W.]
then offered up that he would drop the
upcoming unfair labor practice grievance[2/]
in exchange for detective pay. This is
textbook Quid Pro Quo, which is immoral,
unethical and illegal. I couldn’t believe
what I was hearing to say the least. During
the course of the conversation, he mentioned
that he had spoken to the Mayor and . . . the
[Mayor’s] Chief of Staff on the reasons why
he felt he should get detective pay. He
didn’t elaborate as to their response. The
conversation ended and President [J.W.]
exited . . . . I immediately advised Captain
[J.S.] of the conversation as I couldn’t
believe what was just offered and wanted to
confirm what I was thinking. Captain [J.S.]
agreed that the offer put by President [J.W.]
was Quid Pro Quo or at least not ethical on
its face. On Monday, November 10, 2025, I
advised [the Mayor’s] Chief of Staff . . . of
President [J.W.’s] offer to not file the
unfair labor practice grievance in exchange
for detective pay.
As I am not willing to engage in Quid Pro Quo
and I believe that President [J.W.] knew that
when he left my office on Friday. Can I
assume that this is the unfair labor practice
for which he was trying to solicit unearned
detective pay?
J.W. certifies that during the private conversation (which
he expected to remain private unless mutually agreed otherwise)
J.W. explained to the Police Director that the proposed stipends

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 7.
were proper subjects for negotiations “and/or settlement

the parties (see n.2, supra) as to which the Commission had
encouraged settlement.3/
J.W. further certifies that the Police Director did not
state that the subject was “off limits” or that the bargaining
proposal was “illegal,” and did not otherwise accuse J.W. of
criminal conduct during the November 7 meeting, which ended with
no indication that the Police Director would later do so via
email. J.W. certifies that, given the Police Director’s position
and authority, he understood the email as a warning that he would
be accused of criminal or unethical conduct if he raised these
subjects in bargaining or in meetings with City representatives.
J.W. saw this as an attempt to interfere with and constrain the

these subjects with the City.
J.W. further certifies that such a written accusation by the
Police Director against a law-enforcement supervisor and union
president creates immediate professional jeopardy for the
accused, including credibility implications and the foreseeable
risk that it will be referred for disciplinary action, even if no
3/ J.W. certifies he did not mention or propose to waive or
withdraw another matter (CO-2026-086) during his November 7
meeting with the Police Director, as that UPC had not yet
been filed.

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 8.
discipline has yet been imposed. J.W. certifies that he lacks
personal knowledge of whether the Police Director or any City
official has made any referral to a prosecutor regarding the
allegations in the Police Director’s November 13 email.
J.S. certifies that he is a Captain in the Trenton Police
Department currently serving as the Police Director’s Chief of
Staff, and he is also a dues-paying SOA member. J.S. further
certifies: he was not present and did not witness or overhear any
portion of the private conversation at issue; he did not
independently verify the actual context of President J.W.’s

limited to what the Police Director told him after the fact.
J.S. also certifies that as a sworn Police Captain he has a
duty under the New Jersey Attorney General’s Guidelines and
Department policy to report, investigate, or log credible

certifies that upon receipt of the Police Director’s November 13
email he did not initiate an official inquiry, Internal Affairs
report, or criminal referral regarding President J.W. Based upon
his assessment of available information as well as his training,
experience, and knowledge of the parties’ roles, J.S. saw the
Police Director’s email as characterizing a labor dispute, not a
credible report of criminal activity. Specifically, due to
J.W.’s legal standing as SOA President, J.S. did not interpret

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 9.
the stipend proposal as a criminal act of “extortion” or “illegal
solicitation” that would require law enforcement intervention.
Analysis
Motion for Reconsideration of IR Denial
Motions for reconsideration of interim relief decisions are
governed by N.J.A.C. 19:14-9.6, which states, in pertinent part:
Reconsideration will only be granted based on
a demonstration of extraordinary
circumstances and exceptional importance.
The movant shall specify and bear the burden
of establishing the grounds warranting
reconsideration. . . . The filing and
pendency of a motion for reconsideration
shall not operate to stay the effectiveness
of the Commission’s designee’s interim relief
decision unless otherwise ordered by the
Commission.
Only in cases of exceptional importance will we intrude into the
regular interim relief process by granting a motion for
reconsideration by the full Commission. City of Passaic,
P.E.R.C. No. 2004-50, 30 NJPER 67 (&21 2004); Borough of Closter,
P.E.R.C. No. 2001-75, 27 NJPER 289 (&32104 2001). Interim relief
is an extraordinary remedy to be invoked only in limited
circumstances where appropriate and necessary. State of New
Jersey, P.E.R.C. No. 76-6, 1 NJPER 41 (1975).
To obtain interim relief, the moving party must demonstrate
that it has a substantial likelihood of prevailing in a final
Commission decision on its legal and factual allegations and that
irreparable harm will occur if the requested relief is not

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 10.
granted. Further, the public interest must not be injured by an
interim relief order and the relative hardship to the parties in
granting or denying relief must be considered. Crowe v. De
Gioia, 90 N.J. 126, 132-134 (1982); State of New Jersey (Stockton
State College), P.E.R.C. No. 76-6, 1 NJPER 41 (1975); Little
Egg Harbor Tp., P.E.R.C. No. 94, 1 NJPER 37 (1975). A party
seeking such relief “has the burden to prove each of the Crowe
factors by clear and convincing evidence.” Garden State Equality
v. Dow, 216 N.J. 314, 320 (2013)(emphasis added); Essex Cty.,
P.E.R.C. No. 2005-56, 31 NJPER 103, 106 and n.2 (P45 2005)(all
elements of Crowe test must be present).
Applying the above standards to the record presented, we
deny the SOA’s motion for reconsideration. We sustain the denial
of interim relief because we agree with the Director that the SOA
has not established that it will suffer irreparable harm if the
requested relief is not granted. Harm becomes irreparable in
circumstances where the Commission cannot fashion an adequate
remedy which would return the parties to the conditions that
existed before the occurrence of any unfair practice at the
conclusion of the processing of the unfair practice charge.
Camden Cty. Bd. of Chosen Freeholders, P.E.R.C. No. 2020-60, 47
NJPER 32 (¶6 2020) (citing, City of Newark, I.R. No. 2006-3, 31
NJPER 250 (¶97 2005); Atlantic City Bd. of Ed., I.R. No. 2003-14,
29 NJPER 305 (¶94 2003); and Sussex Cty., I.R. No. 2003-13, 29
NJPER 274 (¶81 2003)).

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 11.
The interim relief sought by the SOA is a retraction of the
Police Director’s November 13 email pending the outcome of the
UPC. If it is determined at the conclusion of the processing of
the UPC that the email violated the Act, such a retraction may be
ordered as part of the overall remedy, thus returning the parties
to conditions that existed before the commission of the unfair
practice.
Further, even assuming (without deciding) that the Police
Director’s email contains an express or implied threat of
discipline for protected activity, the imposition of such
discipline would not constitute irreparable harm where there is
recourse for appeal of that discipline. See, City of Trenton,
I.R. No. 2005-7, 31 NJPER 28 (¶13 2005)(denying IR where “no
discipline had been imposed” on PBA president, “he was still
working and available to represent” employees, and “a
sophisticated [Civil Service] appeal procedure” existed to decide
the legitimacy of then-preliminary disciplinary charges that were
allegedly in retaliation for protected activity). See also,
Bergen Community College, I.R. No. 2008-10, 34 NJPER 58 (¶22
2008) (threat or imposition of discipline does not constitute
irreparable harm); State of New Jersey, I.R. No. 2007-14, 33
NJPER 138 (¶49 2007)(same), recon. granted on other grounds,
P.E.R.C. No. 2008-12, 33 NJPER 225 (¶85 2007); Allentown Bor.,
I.R. No. 2001-14, 27 NJPER 264 (¶32094 2001)(same); Sayreville
Bor., I.R. No. 93-14, 19 NJPER 166 (¶24083 1993)(same). Here,
such disciplinary appeal procedures are available to the SOA,

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 12.
through either the parties’ negotiated grievance procedure (minor
discipline) or the Civil Service (major discipline), as the City
of Trenton is a Civil Service municipality. Trenton City Code,
Art. III, §2-8(A)(1).
Pleading Defects
For purposes of administrative efficiency, we will also
consider whether the SOA’s response to the Director’s January 15
letter has cured any pleading defects. N.J.A.C. 19:14-2.1(a)
sets forth the Commission’s unfair practice complaint issuance
standard, in pertinent part as follows:
[I]f it appears to the Director of Unfair
Practices that the allegations of the charge,
if true, may constitute unfair practices on
the part of the respondent, and that formal
proceedings should be instituted in order to
afford the parties an opportunity to litigate
relevant legal and factual issues, the
Director shall issue and serve a formal
complaint.
[N.J.A.C. 19:14-2.1(a) (emphasis added).]
Our rules also provide that before a complaint issues, the
Director “may permit the charging party to amend a charge upon
such terms as may be deemed just.” N.J.A.C. 19:14-1.5(a).
The SOA responded to the defect letter with an amended UPC
that (on the present record) does not seek complaint issuance on
the section 5.4a(3) and 5.4a(4) claims set forth in its initial
charge. The SOA also provided additional facts and legal
argument. As further explained below, we find the SOA has

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 13.
satisfied the complaint issuance standard as to its section
5.4a(1) claims, but not its 5.4a(5) claim.
The 5.4a(1) Claim
An employer independently violates section 5.4a(1) if its
action tends to interfere with an employee’s statutory rights and
lacks a legitimate and substantial business justification.
Somerville Bd. of Ed., D.U.P. No. 2024-18, 51 NJPER 59, 60 (¶15
2024); N.J. Sports & Exposition Auth., P.E.R.C. No. 80-73, 5
NJPER 550, n.1 (¶10285 1979)). Proof of actual interference,
intimidation, restraint, coercion, or motive is unnecessary; the
objective tendency to interfere is sufficient. Id. (citing,
Commercial Tp. Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 83-25, 8 NJPER 550
(¶13253 1982), aff’d 1983 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 5 (App. Div.
1983); City of Hackensack, P.E.R.C. No. 78-71, 4 NJPER 190 (¶4096
1978), aff’d 1979 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 11 (App. Div. 1979)).
A violation of another unfair practice provision derivatively
violates subsection 5.4a(1). See, e.g., Lakehurst Bd. of Ed.,
P.E.R.C. No. 2004-74, 30 NJPER 186 (¶69 2004), aff’d, 2005 N.J.
Super. Unpub. LEXIS 841 (App. Div. 2005).
Section 5.4a(1) cases require a balancing of two important
but conflicting rights: the employer’s right of free speech and
the employees’ rights to be free from coercion, restraint or
interference in the exercise of protected rights. State of N.J.
(Trenton State Coll.), P.E.R.C. No. 88-19, 13 NJPER 720 (¶18269
1987). In striking that balance, all circumstances of a
particular case must be reviewed. Id. An employer has the right

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 14.
to criticize an employee representative as long as the employer’s
actions do not rise to the level of unlawful interference with
protected rights. Black Horse Pike Reg. Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No.
82-19, 7 NJPER 502 (¶12223 1981). “Unflattering descriptions,
although unfortunate, are sometimes part of both the work and the
labor relations environment. They are not, however, necessarily
illegal.” Lakehurst Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 2004-74, 30 NJPER
186 (¶69 2004), aff’d 31 NJPER 290 (¶113 App. Div. 2005).
The City, having filed no response to the SOA’s IR
application, its motion for reconsideration, or its response to
the defect letter, did not place into the record a legitimate and
substantial business justification for the accusatory statements
in the Police Director’s November 13 email. Nor has the City
disputed the SOA’s certified statements. These include the SOA
President’s view that given his position of authority the Police
Director’s accusation of illegal and unethical conduct created
professional jeopardy for J.W. as a law enforcement officer and
the foreseeable risk of referral for disciplinary action; and
Captain J.S.’s certified opinion that the Police Director’s
accusations against J.W. did not warrant an official inquiry,
Internal Affairs report, or criminal referral.
Further, there is no claim or evidence that J.W. was not
acting in his official capacity as SOA President during the
November 7 meeting, or that the matters under discussion in that
meeting did not concern negotiations over negotiable terms and
conditions of employment. See, e.g., Hamilton Tp. Bd. of Ed.,

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 15.
D.U.P. No. 82-24, 8 NJPER 199 (¶13083 1982) (refusing to issue
complaint on unit members’ charge that association violated its
duty of fair representation when it negotiated multi-year
contract which required withdrawal of certain unfair practice
charges in exchange for certain employer concessions).
Although the Police Director evidently holds a civilian
position, the City’s Administrative Code makes him “directly
responsible for the efficient and routine day-to-day operations
of the Police Department”, with authority to “[a]dopt and
promulgate rules and regulations for the government of the
divisions under his/her supervision and for the discipline of
their members.” Trenton City Code, Art. XII, §2-57(C)(emphasis
added). In light of this significant authority, including over
police disciplinary matters, we find that the allegations in the
SOA’s amended charge, if true, may constitute unfair practices on
the part of the respondent, supporting the issuance of a
complaint under 5.4a(1). That is, further processing of the
charge is required to determine whether the Police Director’s
accusations of illegal and unethical conduct against the SOA
President lacked any legitimate and substantial business
justification.
The 5.4a(5) Claim
The Commission’s standard for determining whether a party
has refused to negotiate in good faith in violation of Section
5.4a(5) of the Act is as follows:

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 16.
It is necessary to subjectively analyze the
totality of the parties’ conduct in order to
determine whether an illegal refusal to
negotiate may have occurred. A determination
that a party has refused to negotiate in good
faith will depend upon an analysis of the
overall conduct and/or attitude of the party
charged. The object of this analysis is to
determine the intent of the respondent, i.e.,
whether the respondent brought to the
negotiating table an open mind and a sincere
desire to reach an agreement, as opposed to a
predetermined intention to go through the
motions, seeking to avoid, rather than reach,
an agreement.
[State of New Jersey, 1 NJPER 39, 40 (1975),
aff’d 141 N.J. Super. 470 (App. Div. 1976).]
Applying that standard here, we find the Police Director’s email
does not evidence a refusal to negotiate requiring the issuance
of a complaint under 5.4a(5). While further processing of the
charge is warranted under 5.4a(1) as detailed supra, the email
contains no explicit refusal to negotiate nor, as the SOA admits,
any assertion by the Police Director to the effect that the
matters under discussion are not negotiable.
The SOA’s certifications do not refute or take specific
issue with the email’s statements that the Police Director agreed
to “hear out” J.W. regarding the proposed stipend for the SOA
President and expressing the Police Director’s view that
“detective pay was only given because one was doing detective
work or one was assigned to the Director’s Office.” The email
further contains the Police Director’s opinion that the reasons
offered by J.W in support of the stipend “are outside of the

PP..EE..RR..CC.. NNOO.. 2026-37 17.
contract or past practice for awarding detective pay.” Overall,
we find that while these statements indicate the parties had
differing viewpoints about the proposal, they are not
inconsistent with good-faith negotiations and do not evince a
“predetermined intention to go through the motions” or avoid,
rather than reach, an agreement.
ORDER
Based upon the foregoing, SOA’s motion for reconsideration
is denied, its 5.4a(5) charge is dismissed, and the matter is
remanded to the Director for complaint issuance and further
processing of its 5.4a(1) claim.

SYNOPSIS
The Public Employment Relations Commission sustains the
Deputy Director of Unfair Practices’ dismissal of an unfair
practice charge (UPC) filed by Kazar against his employer (Board)
and union (UPSEU). The charge alleges that the Board violated
the New Jersey Employer-Employee Relations Act, N.J.S.A.
34:13A-1, et seq., by denying him promotions and accusing him of
“stealing time” after he successfully contested his termination
through grievance arbitration and was reinstated. The charge
alleges that the UPSEU violated the Act by failing to file
grievances or pursue arbitration over his complaints against the
Board and failing to enforce the health benefits reimbursement
portion of the arbitration award that reinstated him. The
Commission finds that all of Kazar’s allegations against the
Board and UPSEU occurred well beyond the six-month statute of
limitations for filing an unfair practice charge. Specifically,
the Commission finds that the alleged failure to comply with or
enforce the health benefits reimbursement of the 2022 arbitration
award was not a continuing violation and that Kazar failed to
file his UPC within six months of the end of the arbitrator’s
jurisdiction over any remaining disputes over remedial relief.
This synopsis is not part of the Commission decision. It
has been prepared for the convenience of the reader. It has been
neither reviewed nor approved by the Commission.

In the Matter of

Appearances:
For the Charging Party, Daniel Kazar, pro se
DECISION
On January 17 and 22, 2026, the Charging Party (Kazar) filed
an appeal and an amended appeal of the Deputy Director of Unfair
Practices’ January 12, 2026 letter dismissing his unfair practice
charge (UPC).1/ Kazar initially filed his UPC on December 26,
2025. After receiving a defect letter from the Deputy Director,
he filed an amended UPC on January 12, 2026.
Kazar’s amended UPC alleges that his employer, the East
Windsor Regional Board of Education (Board), violated subsections
1/ Neither Respondent filed a response to the appeal.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-36 2.
5.4a(1) and (3)2/ of the New Jersey Public Employer-Employee
Relations Act, N.J.S.A. 34:13A-1, et seq. (Act), by retaliating
against him in the form of denying him promotions following his
reinstatement after he successfully contested his November 9,
2019, termination through grievance arbitration. The UPC also
alleges that the Board accused Kazar of “stealing time” as
harassment and retaliation for his reinstatement. The charge
further alleges that Kazar’s union, the United Public Service
Employees Union, Local 424 (UPSEU), violated subsection 5.4b(1)
and 5.4b(5)3/ of the Act by failing to file grievances or pursue
arbitration concerning the Board’s alleged retaliation, failure
to promote, and harassment/false accusation. The UPC also
alleges that the UPSEU arbitrarily, discriminatorily, or in bad
faith failed to enforce a binding arbitration award issued on
February 10, 2022, which reinstated him and ordered remedial
relief.
2/ These provisions prohibit public employers, their
representatives or agents from: “(1) Interfering with,
restraining or coercing employees in the exercise of the
rights guaranteed to them by this act”; and “(3)
Discriminating in regard to hire or tenure of employment or
any term or condition of employment to encourage or
discourage employee in the exercise of the rights guaranteed
to them by the act.”
3/ These provision prohibit employee organizations, their
representatives or agents from: “(1) Interfering with,
restraining or coercing employees in the exercise of the
rights guaranteed to them by this act”; and “(5) Violating
any of the rules and regulations established by the
commission.”

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-36 3.
The Deputy Director’s January 12, 2026 letter dismissed
Kazar’s 5.4b(5) allegation because his UPC did not cite a
Commission rule or regulation that was violated. The Deputy
Director dismissed the remaining allegations for failing to
“provide a clear and concise statement of the facts forming the
basis of your legal and factual claims against the Respondents”
as required by N.J.A.C. 19:14-1.3(a)(3). The Deputy Director
further found that, based on the UPC and amended UPC as is, the
allegations all relate to events occurring between 2019 and 2023
- well beyond the six-month statute of limitations applicable to
a UPC filed December 26, 2025.
The Commission has authority to issue a complaint where it
appears that a charging party’s allegations, if true, may
constitute an unfair practice within the meaning of the Act.
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4c; N.J.A.C. 19:14-2.1. Where no complaint is
issued, the charging party may appeal to the Commission, which
may sustain the refusal to issue a complaint or may direct that
further action be taken. N.J.A.C. 19:14-2.3(b).
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4c establishes a six-month statute of
limitations period for the filing of unfair practice charges.
However, “[t]he Act does not rigidly bar relief on all causes of
action arising more than six months before a charge was filed.”
State of New Jersey (Juvenile Justice) and Judy Thorpe, P.E.R.C.
No. 2014-71, 40 NJPER 512 (¶164 2014), aff’d, 2017 N.J. Super.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-36 4.
Unpub. LEXIS 717, 43 NJPER 353 (¶100 App. Div. 2017), certif.
den. 231 N.J. 211 (2017). A charge may still be filed if the
charging party was “prevented” from filing a charge on time and
the six month period will not begin to run until the charging
party was “no longer so prevented.” N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4c.
Relevant considerations include whether a charging party sought
timely relief in another forum; whether the respondent
fraudulently concealed and misrepresented the facts establishing
an unfair practice; when a charging party knew or should have
known the basis for its claim; and how long a time has passed
between the contested action and the charge. Kaczmarek v. N.J.
Turnpike Auth., 77 N.J. 329, 340 (1978); Lakewood Tp. (Schulman),
P.E.R.C. No. 2020-25, 46 NJPER 234 (¶55 2019); State of New
Jersey, P.E.R.C. No. 2003-56, 29 NJPER 93 (¶26 2003); and Hoboken
Teachers Ass’n, P.E.R.C No. 91-110, 17 NJPER 331(¶22145 1991).
Here, as Kazar’s initial UPC was filed on December 26, 2025,
all allegations against the Board and UPSEU concerning their
actions prior to June 26, 2025 are barred by the statute of
limitations. Specifically, Kazar’s allegations concerning denied
promotions in retaliation for his successful arbitration occurred
in 2021-2022. The allegations concerning false accusations of
stealing time occurred in 2022-2023. As all of those allegations
concern actions well beyond the six-month statute of limitations,
we find them to be untimely pursuant to N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4c.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-36 5.
In his appeal, Kazar asserts that the Board’s alleged
failure to provide him with medical reimbursement as ordered by
the February 10, 2022, arbitration award reinstating him, and the
UPSEU’s alleged failure to seek to enforce that award, are
continuing violations that toll the statute of limitations.
Kazar submitted a copy of the arbitration award along with his
UPC. In addition to ordering his reinstatement, the award
ordered backpay and benefits, including medical reimbursements
for any additional health insurance premiums paid during the
period of separation and any additional out-of-pocket medical
payments. The award was issued on February 10, 2022, and the
arbitrator retained jurisdiction until “May 16, 2022, or until
such other date mutually agreeable, over any remedial relief
issues which remain in dispute between the parties.” Even if the
Board had not provided the medical reimbursements ordered by the
arbitration award, and even if the UPSEU arbitrarily,
discriminatorily, or in bad faith declined to pursue enforcement
on Kazar’s behalf, Kazar would have known of the alleged unfair
practice violations by May 16, 2022, when the arbitrator no
longer retained jurisdiction of remedial relief issues.
Given the nature of the allegations - failure to comply with
(employer) and failure to seek to enforce (union) an aspect of an
arbitration award concerning reimbursement of medical costs
incurred while separated from employment - there is no continuing
violation that would justify tolling the six-month statute of

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-36 6.
limitations. The continuing violation theory is not applicable
where “the claim is not based on new alleged violations, but
rather on the effect of an earlier alleged violation.” State of
N.J. (Dept. of Corrections), P.E.R.C. No. 93-80, 19 NJPER 207
(¶24097 1993); see also Salem Cty., P.E.R.C. No. 87-159, 13 NJPER
584 (¶18216 1987). Once Kazar was reinstated pursuant to the
arbitration award, the alleged medical reimbursement owed was a
past event with a finite amount, not a repeated violation.
Therefore, the alleged failure to comply with or enforce the
arbitration award was a distinct event that should have been
known by the May 16, 2022, date to which the arbitrator retained
jurisdiction. A timely UPC would have needed to be filed within
six months of that date, i.e., by November 16, 2022. As the UPC
was not filed until December 26, 2025, we concur with the Deputy
Director’s determination that his allegations are untimely
pursuant to N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4c. Moreover, Kazar’s submissions
do not demonstrate that he was prevented from timely filing
unfair practice charges concerning his allegations.
ORDER
The Charging Party’s unfair practice charge against the
Board and UPSEU is dismissed.
BY ORDER OF THE COMMISSION
Chair Hennessy-Shotter, Commissioners Davey, Eaton, Higgins,
Hines, and Papero voted in favor of this decision. None opposed.
