P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-35
STATE OF NEW JERSEY
BEFORE THE PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS COMMISSION
In the Matter of
UNIVERSITY HOSPITAL,
Respondent,
-and- Docket No. CI-2026-003
KEVIN PORTER,
Charging Party.
SYNOPSIS
The Public Employment Relations Commission grants Porter’s
appeal of the Director of Unfair Practices’ refusal to issue a
complaint on his unfair practice charge (UPC) against University
Hospital. Porter’s charge alleges that University Hospital
violated the New Jersey Employer-Employee Relations Act, N.J.S.A.
34:13A-1, et seq. when it investigated and disciplined him
following his complaints to management about workplace issues and
his supervisor. The Commission finds that, while some of
Porter’s allegations concern events beyond the statute of
limitations, several of his allegations concern alleged
retaliation for his protected activity occurring within six
months of the filing of his UPC. The Commission remands these
timely allegations to the Director for issuance of a complaint.
This synopsis is not part of the Commission decision. It
has been prepared for the convenience of the reader. It has been
neither reviewed nor approved by the Commission.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-35
STATE OF NEW JERSEY
BEFORE THE PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS COMMISSION
In the Matter of
UNIVERSITY HOSPITAL,
Respondent,
-and- Docket No. CI-2026-003
KEVIN PORTER,
Charging Party.
Appearances:
For the Respondent, University Hospital, Alexandria
Harwin, Associate General Counsel
For the Charging Party, Kevin Porter, pro se
DECISION
On December 12 and 15, 2025, the Charging Party, Kevin
Porter (Porter), filed an appeal and amended appeal of the
December 11, 2025 decision of the Director of Unfair Practices
(Director) refusing to issue a complaint on his unfair practice
charge and amended charges (UPC) filed on July 2, 24, 25, 28, and
29, 2025 against his employer, University Hospital.1/ D.U.P. No.
2026-9, 52 NJPER 179 (¶49 2025). Porter’s UPC alleges that
1/ Porter’s UPC also included allegations against his union,
Teamsters Local 97. However, the Director dismissed those
claims and on August 28, 2025, the Commission denied
Porter’s request for special permission to appeal that
dismissal. P.E.R.C. No. 2026-5, 52 NJPER 85 (¶21 2025).

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-35 2.
University Hospital violated subsections 5.4a(1) and (3)2/ of the
New Jersey Public Employer-Employee Relations Act, N.J.S.A.
34:13A-5.1, et seq. (Act), by retaliating against him in the form
of investigations and discipline following his complaints to
management over issues such as unauthorized employee
reassignments, unequal work distribution caused by
nepotism/favoritism, and threats from a supervisor.
The Director dismissed the majority of Porter’s allegations
as falling outside of the six-month statute of limitations for
filing unfair practice charges. (D.U.P. at 3-5). The Director
dismissed the remaining allegations concerning nepotism and
racial discrimination as being outside of the Commission’s
jurisdiction. (D.U.P. at 5-7). Porter’s amended appeal disputes
the untimeliness finding and asserts that the Director improperly
weighed the evidence and drew adverse conclusions against him
instead of considering whether his allegations, if true, could
constitute an unfair practice. On January 20, 2026, University
Hospital filed a response to Porter’s appeal agreeing with the
2/ These provisions prohibit public employers, their
representatives or agents from: “(1) Interfering with,
restraining or coercing employees in the exercise of the
rights guaranteed to them by this act”; and “(3)
Discriminating in regard to hire or tenure of employment or
any term or condition of employment to encourage or
discourage employee in the exercise of the rights guaranteed
to them by the act.”

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-35 3.
Director’s findings of untimeliness and of lack of jurisdiction
for allegations related to nepotism and racial discrimination.
The Commission has authority to issue a complaint where it
appears that a charging party’s allegations, if true, may
constitute an unfair practice within the meaning of the Act.
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4c; N.J.A.C. 19:14-2.1. Where no complaint is
issued, the charging party may appeal to the Commission, which
may sustain the refusal to issue a complaint or may direct that
further action be taken. N.J.A.C. 19:14-2.3(b).
“An employer violates subsection 5.4a(1) if it engages in
activities which tend to interfere with, restrain or coerce an
employee in the exercise of rights guaranteed by the Act,
provided the actions taken lack a legitimate and substantial
business justification.” Mine Hill Tp., P.E.R.C. No. 86-145, 12
NJPER 526, 527 (¶17197 1986). “For a 5.4a(1) violation to be
found, proof of actual interference, restraint, coercion,
intimidation, or motive is unnecessary; the tendency to interfere
is sufficient.” State of N.J. (Children and Families), P.E.R.C.
No. 2026-18, 52 NJPER 194, 197 (¶52 2025); Trenton Bd. of Ed.,
P.E.R.C. No. 2023-45, 49 NJPER 530 (¶126 2023); and Commercial
Tp. Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 83-25, 8 NJPER 550, 552 (¶13253
1982), aff’d, 1983 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 5, 10 NJPER 78
(¶15043 App. Div. 1983).

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-35 4.
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4a(3) prohibits public employers, their
representatives, or agents, from: “Discriminating in regard to
hire or tenure of employment or any term or condition of
employment to encourage or discourage employees in the exercise
of the rights guaranteed to them by this act.” Allegations of
anti-union discrimination under N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4a(3) are
governed by In re Bridgewater Tp., 95 N.J. 235, 240-246 (1984).
Bridgewater established that the charging party must prove, by a
preponderance of the evidence on the entire record, that
protected conduct was a substantial or motivating factor in the
adverse action. This may be done by direct evidence or by
circumstantial evidence showing that the employee engaged in
protected activity, the employer knew of this activity, and the
employer was hostile toward the exercise of the protected rights.
Id. at 246. If the employer did not present any evidence of a
motive not illegal under our Act, or if its explanation has been
rejected as pretextual, there is sufficient basis for finding a
violation without further analysis. Id. at 241. Sometimes,
however, the record demonstrates that both motives unlawful under
our Act and other motives contributed to a personnel action. In
these dual motive cases, the employer will not have violated the
Act if it can prove, by a preponderance of the evidence on the
entire record, that the adverse action would have taken place
absent the protected conduct. Id. at 242.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-35 5.
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4c establishes a six-month statute of
limitations period for the filing of unfair practice charges.
However, “[t]he Act does not rigidly bar relief on all causes of
action arising more than six months before a charge was filed.”
State of New Jersey (Juvenile Justice) and Judy Thorpe, P.E.R.C.
No. 2014-71, 40 NJPER 512 (¶164 2014), aff’d, 2017 N.J. Super.
Unpub. LEXIS 717, 43 NJPER 353 (¶100 App. Div. 2017), certif.
den. 231 N.J. 211 (2017). A charge may still be filed if the
charging party was “prevented” from filing a charge on time and
the six month period will not begin to run until the charging
party was “no longer so prevented.” N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4c.
Relevant considerations include whether a charging party sought
timely relief in another forum; whether the respondent
fraudulently concealed and misrepresented the facts establishing
an unfair practice; when a charging party knew or should have
known the basis for its claim; and how long a time has passed
between the contested action and the charge. Kaczmarek v. N.J.
Turnpike Auth., 77 N.J. 329, 340 (1978); Lakewood Tp. (Schulman),
P.E.R.C. No. 2020-25, 46 NJPER 234 (¶55 2019); State of New
Jersey, P.E.R.C. No. 2003-56, 29 NJPER 93 (¶26 2003); and Hoboken
Teachers Ass’n, P.E.R.C No. 91-110, 17 NJPER 331 (¶22145 1991).
Here, as Porter’s initial UPC was filed on July 2, 2025, all
allegations of retaliation for protected activity occurring prior
to January 2, 2025 are barred by the statute of limitations.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-35 6.
Specifically, for example, the June 19, 2024, discipline Porter
alleges was in retaliation for advocating for employee rights
occurred more than six months prior to his July 2, 2025, UPC.
(D.U.P. at 3). Porter’s allegations of retaliation immediately
following his September 30, 2024 complaints to management also
occurred outside of the six month statute of limitations. Id.
Moreover, Porter’s submissions do not demonstrate that he was
prevented from timely filing unfair practice charges concerning
those allegations. We therefore concur with the Director’s
determination that those allegations are untimely pursuant to
N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4c. (D.U.P. at 4-5).
We next address the substantive question of whether a
complaint should issue on any allegations contained in Porter’s
UPC occurring within the six-month statute of limitations
(January 2, 2025, or later). Initially, we concur with the
Director’s determination that Porter’s racial discrimination
allegations must be dismissed because the Commission does not
have jurisdiction over civil rights claims. State of N.J.
(Kearny), P.E.R.C. No. 2025-19, 51 NJPER 175 (¶44 2024); and
Woodstown-Pilesgrove Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 2023-18, 49 NJPER
273 (¶63 2022). Claims of anti-union discrimination cannot be
based on alleged violations of laws other than the Act,
particularly where those laws provide a forum for review of an
employer’s actions. N.J. Turnpike Auth., P.E.R.C. No. 2022-38,

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-35 7.
48 NJPER 393 (¶90 2022); and Elizabeth Housing Auth. (Looney),
P.E.R.C. No. 90-84, 16 NJPER 211 (¶21084 1990).
We also concur with the Director’s determination that
Porter’s nepotism hiring claim, standing alone, does not
implicate the Commission’s unfair practice jurisdiction. (D.U.P.
at 6); see UMDNJ, H.E. No. 90-13, 15 NJPER 632 (¶20266 1989),
adopted, P.E.R.C. No. 90-51, 16 NJPER 12 (¶21007 1989)
(favoritism, standing alone, in selecting a certain employee for
a supervisory training course and promoting her did not violate
the Act where it was not shown to be in retaliation for protected
activity of employees not selected or to repudiate the CNA’s
promotional procedures). Furthermore, as Porter does not allege
that he applied for the position allegedly filled by his
supervisor’s relative in March 2025 (and stated in his July 29,
2025 UPC that it was for a “position identical” to his), there is
no viable unfair practice claim that Porter was denied the
position in retaliation for protected activity. Compare Bergen
Cty. Special Services School Dist., P.E.R.C. No. 88-83, 14 NJPER
241 (¶19088 1988), aff’d, 1989 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 5, NJPER
Supp.2d 206 (¶181 App. Div. 1989) (employer violated the Act when
it retaliated against an employee for his protected conduct by
applying altered criteria to hire a different candidate than him
for a full-time interpreter position).

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-35 8.
However, we disagree with the Director’s conclusion that
Porter does not allege “that he was affected in any way by the
alleged nepotism hire.” (D.U.P. at 6). Porter’s July 23, 2025,
amended UPC alleges that a Navigator (Y.M.) with supervisory
authority to assign work engaged in favoritism towards her
daughter-in-law (or son’s girlfriend), causing unequal
distribution of work. See Bloomingdale Bor., H.E. No. 2006-2, 31
NJPER 267 (¶106 2005) (employee “established that [he] was
engaged in a protected activity” when he argued with his
supervisor over “alleged favoritism towards some employees
regarding terms and conditions of employment”). Porter also
alleged that Y.M. “threatened” him at work in violation of
University Hospital’s employee conduct policy. The UPC alleges
that on June 24, 2025, Porter expressed these concerns about Y.M.
to Human Resources and was told that he was under investigation.
He asserts this was “retaliation for speaking out.”
Porter’s July 25, 2025, amended UPC claimed violations of
subsections 5.4a(1) and 5.4a(3) of the Act while reiterating his
allegations about the June 24, 2025, meeting with HR, stating:
“In June 2025, I made additional internal complaints after
retaliation escalated. On June 24, 2025, when I asked HR about
prior complaints, I was told they had not been reviewed and
instead was informed I was under investigation - demonstrating
retaliation for protected activity.”

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-35 9.
Additionally, Porter’s July 28, 2025, amended UPC alleged
that on January 3, 2025, he “reported misconduct involving
unauthorized reassignments and CBA violations at University
Hospital” including submission of a communication from a former
union representative stating that “employees could not be
arbitrarily reassigned without union involvement.” He alleges
that on February 5, 2025, he was “issued a disciplinary warning
by Supervisor [Y.M.] who accused [him] of ‘misuse’ of the union
document.” Porter alleges this disciplinary “write-up was
directly connected to my protected conduct and constituted
retaliatory action in violation of N.J.S.A. 34:13A-5.4(a)(3).”
We find that these portions of Porter’s amended unfair
practice charges assert retaliation for protected activities
including complaints of threats by a supervisor in violation of
the employee conduct policy, complaints of unauthorized
reassignments in violation of the CNA, and complaints of unequal
work distribution caused by nepotism/favoritism. “Protected
activity under the Act may include individual conduct – such as
complaints, arguments, objections, letters or similar activity -
related to enforcing a collective negotiations agreement or
preserving or protesting working conditions of employees in a
recognized or certified unit.” Jackson Tp., P.E.R.C. No.
2022-50, 49 NJPER 55, 58 (¶11 2022); Bloomfield Tp., P.E.R.C. No.
2025-26, 51 NJPER 242 (¶57 2025); Saddle River Bd. of Ed.,

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-35 10.
P.E.R.C. No. 2025-12, 51 NJPER 135 (¶34 2024); State of N.J.,
P.E.R.C. No. 2006-11, 31 NJPER 276 (¶109 2005); and North
Brunswick Tp. Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 79-14, 4 NJPER 451 (¶4205
1978), aff’d, 1979 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 13, NJPER Supp.2d 63
(¶45 App. Div. 1979).
An employer will violate subsection 5.4a(3) of the Act if it
disciplines an employee in retaliation for protected activity.
See, e.g., Belleville Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 2015-79, 42 NJPER
41 (¶12 2015), aff’d, 455 N.J. Super. 387 (App. Div. 2018)
(employer violated Act by imposing discipline on a teacher
disproportionate to his alleged misconduct in retaliation for
expressing union’s concerns about security system); Middletown
Tp. Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 96-45, 22 NJPER 31 (¶27016 1995),
aff’d, 1996 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 8, 23 NJPER 53 (¶28036 App.
Div. 1996), certif. denied, 149 N.J. 35 (1997) (employer violated
Act when it disciplined a teacher for criticizing the
superintendent); and New Brunswick Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 2024-
34, 50 NJPER 318 (¶77 2024) (employer violated Act by
disciplining union representative in retaliation for arguing with
principal about several workplace issues).
We therefore find that Porter’s UPC contains several
allegations that fall within the six-month statute of limitations
and concern retaliation for protected activity under the Act. In
accordance with our complaint issuance standard, we find that it

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-35 11.
appears that the allegations of the charge, if true, may
constitute unfair practices on the part of University Hospital,
requiring formal proceedings in order to afford the parties an
opportunity to litigate relevant legal and factual issues.
N.J.A.C. 19:14-2.1. Accordingly, we remand to the Director for
the issuance of a complaint on Porter’s 5.4a(1) and 5.4a(3)
charges pertaining to the above-identified allegations that are
not barred by the statute of limitations. See, e.g., Jackson
Tp., P.E.R.C. No. 2022-50, supra (Commission remanded UPC to
Director for issuance of a complaint on allegation that employer
laid off employee in retaliation for his advocacy for himself and
other employees related to terms and conditions of employment);
and Essex Cty., P.E.R.C. No. 2023-29, 49 NJPER 365 (¶88 2023)
(Commission remanded UPC to Director for issuance of a complaint
on allegation that employer threatened employee with discipline
for speech he made to union members).
ORDER
The unfair practice charge is remanded to the Director of
Unfair Practices for issuance of a Complaint on Porter’s 5.4a(1)
and 5.4a(3) charges consistent with this decision.
